topics.title: Start Here
topics.summary: You can build a CRUD app. What comes next? How to use this platform, and what architecture really is, in five minutes.

slides.title: Read it, got it… forgot it
slides.tldr: Reading alone fades within a week. To remember something, you have to keep asking yourself about it.

slides.title: The four-step learning loop
slides.tldr: See → recall → check → come back. This loop is what turns small pieces of knowledge into lasting ones.

slides.title: The three rooms of the platform
slides.tldr: Lesson teaches with slides, Flashcards make you recall, and Quiz checks you.

slides.title: From a coffee cart to a big restaurant
slides.tldr: Code that runs fine for 10 users can break at 10,000 — not because the code was wrong, but because the pressure changed.

slides.title: The last ticket sold twice
slides.tldr: "Check first, then change" code goes wrong when two requests arrive together — the best-known trap in CRUD apps. The next slide fixes it.

slides.title: Check and book in one step
slides.tldr: Move the check into the write itself: one UPDATE that only succeeds while the seat is still free, then read how many rows changed.

slides.title: So what is architecture?
slides.tldr: Architecture is the set of decisions that cost the most to change later.

slides.title: A map of the whole course
slides.tldr: A request travels from the user to the database along one path, and each topic in the course covers one stop on that path.

topics.title: Architectural Thinking
topics.summary: Which decisions are hard to undo and which are cheap, and how to weigh trade-offs before you commit.

slides.title: Three days on dark mode, five minutes on the parcel ID
slides.tldr: Teams pour days into decisions that could wait and settle expensive ones in five minutes, because they never learned to tell which is which.

slides.title: The touchstone: what will it cost to change later?
slides.tldr: Three questions tell you if a decision is architectural: how much stands on it, whether data has piled up, and whether outsiders use it.

slides.title: Four familiar foundations — and the things that are just paint
slides.tldr: Stop for the database choice, the data model, service boundaries and the public API contract; move fast on most other decisions.

slides.title: Sorting a feature's decisions
slides.tldr: List every decision in the feature and put its cost of change beside it: minutes, days, weeks, months. Spend your time only on weeks and months.

slides.title: Turning paint into a foundation by accident
slides.tldr: Return an entity as JSON and your table columns become the public contract; a separate response class keeps the inside cheap to change.

slides.title: An hour on a banner color, one minute to drop a column
slides.tldr: Teams spend time on decisions that are easy to undo, and rush through the ones that can't be undone.

slides.title: Which kind of door is it — and how fast to move
slides.tldr: Decide reversible things fast; decide irreversible ones slowly and in writing. The cost of going back is what tells them apart.

slides.title: Turning a one-way door into a two-way door
slides.tldr: Hide a big decision behind an interface and a feature flag, so you can go back to the old code path if it goes wrong. The flag does not undo data.

slides.title: The drop-column trap: four steps instead of one
slides.tldr: Changing code and dropping a column in one deploy cuts off your way back; remove it in four steps: expand, migrate, switch, contract.

slides.title: Expand and contract, in real code
slides.tldr: Step 1-2 is one additive migration plus a dual write in the entity; the drop waits for its own deploy and a zero-row check.

slides.title: A loan taken in the Black Friday rush, with interest six months later
slides.tldr: A rushed job left unfixed piles up like a loan, and the interest is that every new feature gets a little slower.

slides.title: Two kinds of debt: knowing and unknowing
slides.tldr: Debt taken on knowingly, with a repayment plan, is a tactic; debt that piles up unnoticed or ignored is the real danger.

slides.title: The debt ledger: where to write it and how
slides.tldr: Write a one-page entry for each debt: what, why, interest, repayment terms and date; leave a marker with a ticket number in the code.

slides.title: Three habits for paying off debt
slides.tldr: Fix small debts whenever you touch them (boy scout rule), set aside time each sprint for big ones, and pick the debt with the highest interest.

slides.title: Repaying DEBT-12: merge the copy into one class
slides.tldr: Pin today's totals with a test, then merge the two classes: the one real difference becomes a small injected policy, and the shared rules live once.

slides.title: A team of 10, 12 services
slides.tldr: A small team that splits into 12 services on day one gets none of the benefits, only the extra burden of networks, deploys and debugging.

slides.title: Three shapes: monolith, modular monolith, microservices
slides.tldr: A monolith is one lump, a modular monolith has separate rooms in one house, and microservices are separate houses; the real difference is how firm the boundaries are.

slides.title: Building a modular monolith in Symfony
slides.tldr: Under src/, make a folder per business capability, give each an Api interface, and hold only IDs, not other modules' entities.

slides.title: The shortcut that quietly ends the modular monolith
slides.tldr: A Doctrine relation or a repository call across modules ties them together. Keep only an ID, ask through the Api, and let a tool fail the build on shortcuts.

slides.title: Where to draw boundaries, and when to split into services
slides.tldr: Draw boundaries by business capability and data ownership, not by technical layer; split into a service only when you need a separate team and separate scaling.

slides.title: A 600-line controller: afraid to change the discount rule
slides.tldr: When HTTP, SQL, business rules and email are mixed in one controller, even a tiny rule change means understanding the whole file.

slides.title: Three layers, and one direction of dependency
slides.tldr: The controller knows only HTTP, the service holds business rules, the repository fetches and stores data; and dependencies run only from top to bottom.

slides.title: Arranging three layers in Symfony
slides.tldr: The controller only binds a DTO and calls a service; the service runs the rules and uses a repository interface, with Doctrine underneath.

slides.title: Moving off legacy: the strangler fig, piece by piece
slides.tldr: Put a router in front of the old app without shutting it down, move one path at a time to new code, and delete the old code at the end.

slides.title: Two apps, one database, one login
slides.tldr: While both apps run they share the database and the login cookie. Change shared data by adding before removing, and let the new app ask the old one who is logged in.

slides.title: Anti-corruption layer: keep the old system's odd language out
slides.tldr: Don't let the legacy system's odd names and formats into new code; confine them to one translator class.

slides.title: Add a second server and users get logged out
slides.tldr: If sessions and uploaded files live on one server's disk, adding a second server means users are logged in one minute and logged out the next.

slides.title: Stateless means: memory lives outside the server
slides.tldr: A stateless server remembers nothing itself, so any server can handle any request; the memory lives in the database, Redis or object storage.

slides.title: Two steps to make Symfony stateless
slides.tldr: Send sessions to Redis with one line of config, and write uploads through a Flysystem storage instead of the local disk. The storage config is on the next slide.

slides.title: Point the storage name at S3 (and at disk in dev)
slides.tldr: One Flysystem config says what stands behind the storage name: S3 in production, a local folder in dev. The upload code never changes.

slides.title: Serverless: like a taxi, you pay per ride
slides.tldr: With serverless the platform runs the servers and you pay for what you use; in return you accept cold starts and limits.

slides.title: When serverless fits, and when it doesn't
slides.tldr: For bursty or irregular work serverless is cheap and easy; for heavy, constant or long-running work your own servers or containers are better.

slides.title: "Fast, always up, secure, and cheap, please"
slides.tldr: Asking for the maximum of everything isn't a requirement, it's a decision avoided; and vague wishes can't be measured, so nobody knows when the work is done.

slides.title: Five qualities, and each one is paid for by another
slides.tldr: Speed, availability, security, maintainability and cost can't all be maxed out together; raising one lowers another.

slides.title: Turn vague wishes into numbers
slides.tldr: Write each quality as a scenario, a measure and a target, and everyone can tell whether the work is done.

slides.title: Pick the top two first, then put limits on the rest
slides.tldr: For each system pick the two most important qualities, set a minimum bar for the others, and keep the price of each extra "nine" in mind.

slides.title: How much rice for a 500-guest wedding?
slides.tldr: You don't need an exact answer; two minutes of rough math on a scrap of paper catches a 10x mistake, and that is enough to decide.

slides.title: From users to servers: a chain of multiplications
slides.tldr: Multiply users by requests each, divide by 86,400 to get QPS, apply a peak factor, then divide by what one server can handle.

slides.title: The few numbers worth memorizing
slides.tldr: Knowing the time conversions (1 day is about 100,000 seconds), size units and a few latency magnitudes lets you do the math in your head.

slides.title: The whole sum once: a package tracking app
slides.tldr: For one app: QPS, servers, storage, bandwidth, memory and cost on one sheet. The answer is modest: about 3 servers, not 50 and not 1.

slides.title: Four traps in estimation
slides.tldr: Forgetting peak load, forgetting replicas and indexes, treating assumptions as facts, and showing false precision are what ruin estimates.

slides.title: Five hundred users, six technologies
slides.tldr: Every new technology brings the cost of running it for life, not just of installing it, and a small team sinks under that weight.

slides.title: The complexity budget and boring technology
slides.tldr: A team's attention is a limited budget: spend it on new technology only where it moves the business forward, and use familiar tools everywhere else.

slides.title: Three roads: build, buy, open source
slides.tldr: Build what sets your business apart, buy what everyone needs in the same way, and take open source when you can run a mature tool.

slides.title: TCO: working out the real three-year price
slides.tldr: The price isn't just the license or the monthly bill: setup + running + people's time + exit cost. Compare three-year totals.

slides.title: You bought it, but left no exit door
slides.tldr: If a vendor's SDK spreads across your code, switching vendors is nearly impossible; behind an interface, the change happens in one place.

segments.title: Choosing a stack for the job

slides.title: Two teams, two stacks, two kinds of pain
slides.tldr: Both teams picked a stack by fashion or habit instead of by the job, and each paid for it in the part of the system that mattered most.

slides.title: Start from the job: six questions
slides.tldr: Write down what the application needs first (workload, correctness, built-ins, integrations, people, support), then see which stack fits, not the other way around.

slides.title: Worked example: a video site and an insurance system
slides.tldr: Ask the same six questions of both jobs. The answers differ, so what you look for in a stack differs, and several stacks can still fit either job.

slides.title: Built in, or build it yourself?
slides.tldr: Mature stacks ship transactions, security, batch and scheduling ready-made. Check what yours ships before you hand-build it, and know what that convenience costs.

slides.title: The trap: a fashionable rewrite or a benchmark winner
slides.tldr: Rewriting a working system into a trendy stack, or choosing by one speed benchmark, spends your complexity budget on a problem you never measured.

slides.title: One coupon feature, three teams' queues
slides.tldr: Work follows the way teams are split: with teams divided by layer, even a small feature waits in three queues.

slides.title: As the teams are, so is the system
slides.tldr: Conway's Law: a system is built along the lines of how the organization communicates, so system boundaries are a shadow of team boundaries.

slides.title: The other way around: system first, then teams
slides.tldr: The inverse Conway maneuver: arrange teams along the architecture you want, with one owner and one written contract for each boundary.

slides.title: When teams and services don't line up
slides.tldr: Three teams on one service, or one team with eight services: both are wrong; and changing only the org chart doesn't change the code.

slides.title: Redrawing boundaries: eight services, three modules
slides.tldr: To redraw boundaries, list which services each recent feature touched; the ones that always change together become one module with one owner.

slides.title: Rules on paper, code that quietly drifts
slides.tldr: If an architecture rule lives only in a document, the code drifts away from it unnoticed until the damage is big.

slides.title: Fitness functions: rules that test themselves
slides.tldr: A fitness function is an automated check that measures an architectural quality or rule and runs in CI. Break the rule and the build goes red.

slides.title: Guarding with Deptrac and a query budget
slides.tldr: Describe layers (the Doctrine library too) and permissions in deptrac.yaml, put a query-count limit in PHPUnit, and run both in CI. A violation blocks the merge.

slides.title: A violation caught, and the fix
slides.tldr: A developer maps a Domain class with Doctrine attributes; Deptrac turns CI red; moving the mapping to Infrastructure fixes it. Guard only rules worth the upkeep.

slides.title: The last responsible moment: when to decide?
slides.tldr: Postpone hard-to-reverse decisions as long as waiting costs nothing, because that is when you know the most. But without a trigger, "later" never comes.

slides.title: What the design doesn't say is what bites
slides.tldr: Every design document describes the happy path. The breakages hide in the unstated assumptions, and a reviewer's job is to drag them into the open.

slides.title: The four-question checklist
slides.tldr: Ask four questions at every step: what if it fails, what if it arrives twice, what if it is slow, what if we run it again? A good review starts here.

slides.title: A design review, hands on
slides.tldr: Ask the four questions of the happy-path checkout code to find four gaps, then fix the code for each and write review comments that carry the question.

slides.title: Pre-mortem: stage the failure in advance
slides.tldr: A review fails when everyone looks only at the happy path. In a pre-mortem you assume the project has already sunk, then hunt for the reasons.

slides.title: The service that is wired to everything
slides.tldr: When business rules are tangled directly into Doctrine, an SMS vendor and a payment client, tests are slow and switching a vendor is misery.

slides.title: Ports and adapters: the phone's charging port
slides.tldr: The rules sit in the middle and ask the outside world for things through interfaces (ports). The database, SMS and HTTP are adapters of those interfaces, and dependencies point from outside in.

slides.title: Ports, use cases and adapters in Symfony
slides.tldr: Write the interface on the inside, inject it into the use case, and write the Doctrine or Notifier adapter on the outside. `#[AsAlias]` lets autowiring match them up.

slides.title: Testing without a database, swapping a vendor in one class
slides.tldr: An in-memory fake of a port makes rule tests run in milliseconds, and a new vendor just means one new adapter class.

slides.title: The port that leaks the equipment's name
slides.tldr: When QueryBuilder or a vendor type shows up in a port, the inside gets tangled with the equipment again. Name and type the port in business language.

segments.title: DDD: code in the language of the business

slides.title: The business speaks one language, the code another
slides.tldr: When the business and the developers don't use the same words, misunderstandings seep into the code. A ubiquitous language is one shared vocabulary, and the code uses it too.

slides.title: Turn the business sentence into a method name
slides.tldr: Give each business sentence its own method, named in the business's words, with the rule inside. A refund after a customer cancellation then looks wrong at a glance.

slides.title: Bounded context: one word, one meaning, one boundary
slides.tldr: In a big system the same word means different things in different places. Draw a boundary (a bounded context) around each meaning, and keep one meaning per word inside it.

slides.title: Entity and value object
slides.tldr: An entity is recognized by its identity (id), a value object by its value. Make things like money and addresses value objects and the rules become safe on their own.

slides.title: What goes wrong with float money and raw strings
slides.tldr: A float or a raw string accepts anything, so mistakes slip in silently. A Money or Email object refuses wrong values at the door.

slides.title: Aggregate: the boundary that guards the rules
slides.tldr: Make the things that change together into one aggregate and let its root guard the rules. If outside code changes the inner parts directly, the rules break.

segments.title: Event-driven and CQRS at a glance

slides.title: When checkout calls everyone itself
slides.tldr: If you finish a job and then call everyone else one by one, adding anything new means touching checkout, and one slow service slows everybody.

slides.title: Event-driven: pin it to the notice board
slides.tldr: Event-driven means that when the work is done, you just announce what happened. Whoever cares listens and does their own job, and the announcer never needs to know who they are.

slides.title: CQRS: the checkout log and the catalog
slides.tldr: CQRS splits writing (rules) from reading (speed) into separate models. A list page that needed 21 queries becomes one flat query.

slides.title: Events and handlers in Symfony
slides.tldr: Create separate command.bus and event.bus in Messenger, make events small past-tense readonly classes, and let listeners hear them with #[AsMessageHandler].

slides.title: A crash between save and announce loses the event
slides.tldr: If the server dies after saving the order but before dispatching the event, nothing is announced. Store the event in the same database transaction and send it from a worker.

slides.title: When it pays off, and what it costs
slides.tldr: Event-driven and CQRS loosen boundaries and add speed, at the price of harder debugging, eventual consistency and more code. Adopt them only once the need is proven.

segments.title: Writing designs down: C4, sequence, ADR

slides.title: The newcomer's question nobody can answer
slides.tldr: If a system's structure and the reasons behind its decisions live only in people's heads, the knowledge leaves when they do. Three tools capture it: C4, sequence diagrams and ADRs.

slides.title: C4: four zoom levels, like a map
slides.tldr: C4 draws a system at four levels: Context, Container, Component and Code. It works like zooming a map, and each diagram shows exactly one zoom level.

slides.title: Sequence diagram: what happens in order
slides.tldr: C4 shows who knows whom; a sequence diagram shows what happens in what order, including the failure branch that box-and-arrow pictures miss.

slides.title: ADR: the record of a decision
slides.tldr: An ADR (Architecture Decision Record) is a short file with the context, the decision, the alternatives and the consequences. Once written it is not edited; a new ADR supersedes an old one.

slides.title: Documents that go stale
slides.tldr: A wiki diagram drifts from the code and goes stale in two years. Keep diagrams and ADRs beside the code in the repository, and they get updated in the same pull request.

topics.title: API Design
topics.summary: The path a request travels, where it breaks, and how to design an API that still holds up years later.

segments.title: The full journey of a request

slides.title: Empty logs, site down
slides.tldr: A request passes through many hands before it reaches your Symfony code. If it breaks along the way, your log knows nothing about it.

slides.title: Six hops before the answer
slides.tldr: Client → DNS → CDN → load balancer → service → datastore. Each hop has its own job, and the answer comes back along the same road in reverse.

slides.title: What the user sees when each hop breaks
slides.tldr: Every hop breaks in its own way: name not found, 502/503/504, 500 or an endless spinner. The symptom tells you which hop failed.

slides.title: Spotting the broken hop in client code
slides.tldr: In the Vue client, sort failures into no response, timeout, gateway 5xx, app 5xx and your own mistake, and show a different message for each.

slides.title: Every user shows the same IP
slides.tldr: Behind a load balancer, Symfony can't see the real client IP or HTTPS unless you tell it, with trusted_proxies, whom to believe.

slides.title: One renamed field, 30,000 blank phones
slides.tldr: Many clients read your API response, known and unknown. Rename one field and the old clients quietly break.

slides.title: Which changes are safe, which break
slides.tldr: Adding something new is safe; renaming, deleting or changing a type breaks. If readers ignore fields they don't know, both sides can grow in peace.

slides.title: Renaming safely: send both for a while
slides.tldr: To rename a field without blanking old phones, add the new name, keep the old one, wait until nobody reads it, then remove it.

slides.title: When you must break: which versioning method
slides.tldr: If you can't avoid a break, ship a new version. The simplest and most common method is /v1, /v2 in the URL. The real work is keeping one set of logic under both versions.

slides.title: A safe way to retire an old version
slides.tldr: Never switch it off suddenly. Announce it, send Deprecation and Sunset headers, measure who still uses it, and shut it down only when the date arrives.

slides.title: The test that changes along with the code
slides.tldr: The developer who changes a field also changes the test, so the break goes unnoticed. A contract test guards, separately, what old clients rely on.

slides.title: One phone screen, five requests
slides.tldr: No single API style fits every job. On a small mobile screen you sometimes get far more data than you need, and sometimes have to call again and again for one screen.

slides.title: Four ways to order food
slides.tldr: REST is a fixed menu, GraphQL is building your own plate, gRPC is a walkie-talkie to the kitchen, and a message is leaving a note: four styles, four different strengths.

slides.title: What GraphQL and gRPC look like
slides.tldr: In GraphQL the client writes exactly what it wants and fetches it in one go. In gRPC the .proto file is the contract, and a field's number can never change.

slides.title: The pain gRPC cures: a renamed field
slides.tldr: Between two internal services, hand-written JSON drifts apart without a sound. A shared .proto turns the same rename into a loud failure before deploy.

slides.title: The style that doesn't make you wait: 202 Accepted
slides.tldr: For slow work, take the request, answer at once with 202 and a status URL; a Messenger worker does the job in the background and the client asks later.

slides.title: Which one, and when: a decision chart
slides.tldr: Choose by situation: REST for public and ordinary work, GraphQL for complex screens across many clients, gRPC between internal services, messages for slow work.

slides.title: Page 5000 takes 3 seconds
slides.tldr: Paginating with OFFSET gets slower the deeper you go, and when new data arrives the pages shift, so rows go missing or show up twice.

slides.title: A bookmark: start after the last row
slides.tldr: Cursor (keyset) pagination remembers the value of the last row you saw and asks for "the 20 after that one". The index jumps straight there, so every page is equally fast.

slides.title: A keyset query in Doctrine
slides.tldr: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC, and the next-page condition (created_at < :at) OR (created_at = :at AND id < :id). Fetch one extra row to learn whether there is more.

slides.title: From controller to Vue: passing the cursor along
slides.tldr: The controller returns items and nextCursor. Vue sends that nextCursor back as after in the next request, and stops when it gets null.

slides.title: When rows with the same timestamp vanish
slides.tldr: If the cursor is built on created_at alone, rows from the same second get lost at the page boundary. Add a unique tie-breaker (id) to the ordering.

slides.title: "Something went wrong"
slides.tldr: If every error is a meaningless message, or hidden inside a 200 OK, the client can do nothing: not fix it, not retry, not even stop.

slides.title: Status codes, like a courier's return slip
slides.tldr: 2xx is success, 4xx is your (the client's) mistake, 5xx is our (the server's) mistake. Each code says whose fault it is, and whether sending again can help.

slides.title: One error shape everybody knows: problem+json
slides.tldr: Return every error in one mould, the application/problem+json shape from RFC 9457: type, title, status, detail, plus your own machine-readable code.

slides.title: Validation errors: what is wrong in which field
slides.tldr: Return all the mistakes in a form at once, each with its field, a machine-readable code and a message, so the client can show the right error beside each input.

slides.title: Blind retry: charged twice
slides.tldr: Retry only errors that are temporary, and only work that does no harm if done twice. GET, PUT and DELETE are safe; POST isn't, unless there is an idempotency key.

slides.title: The fix: the same key on every retry
slides.tldr: The client makes one Idempotency-Key per user action and reuses it on every retry. The server runs the job once per key and replays the saved answer.

slides.title: One person's loop slows the site for everyone
slides.tldr: When one client (a buggy loop, a scraper, a malicious bot) fires thousands of requests, everyone else's answers slow down. With no limit, one mistake can take the whole API down.

slides.title: The food truck's ready plates: token bucket
slides.tldr: Token bucket: tokens collect in a bucket over time, each request spends one, and when the bucket is empty you wait. Short bursts pass, sustained pressure is stopped.

slides.title: Adding a limit with Symfony RateLimiter
slides.tldr: Give a policy, limit and rate under framework.rate_limiter; in a listener, call consume() with the client's key; past the limit, throw TooManyRequestsHttpException.

slides.title: What a client does on a 429
slides.tldr: The server sends 429 and Retry-After. The client obeys that time, and if it is missing, retries with exponential backoff and jitter (a random delay).

slides.title: Limit whom: IP, user or key
slides.tldr: Limit by IP and the thousand users of one mobile carrier count as one person. Use the user id or API key where you can, and a strict separate limit where it matters, like login.

segments.title: Business logic belongs on the server

slides.title: The same phone, three prices
slides.tldr: If the discount or price calculation lives in the client's code, every client gives a different answer, and users can change that calculation themselves before sending it.

slides.title: The client shows, the server decides
slides.tldr: Business decisions (price, permissions, rules) are written once on the server. The client only shows the result and does small up-front checks for the user's convenience.

slides.title: The server builds the price, the client only sends items
slides.tldr: The client sends only the product id and quantity. The server works out the price, discount and total from its own database and returns them.

slides.title: Checkout end to end: the tampered total is ignored
slides.tldr: The controller reads only product ids and quantities, gets a Quote from PriceCalculator, saves it and returns the numbers; a total changed in DevTools is never read.

slides.title: Who decides whether to show the button
slides.tldr: The permission rule lives on the server (a Voter). Send `abilities` flags in the response and the client shows or hides buttons from them; the server checks again on the real action.

slides.title: BFF: the shape changes, not the rules
slides.tldr: A Backend for Frontend joins and trims data to fit each client's screen. The business rules still stay in the core server, not in the BFF.

topics.title: Databases & Data
topics.summary: Which database for which job, how indexes work, what changes as data grows, and changing a schema without downtime.

slides.title: A popular database, the wrong job
slides.tldr: Pick a database by how your data will be written and queried, not by what is trendy right now.

slides.title: Six kinds of databases, six kinds of notebooks
slides.tldr: Relational, document, key-value, wide-column, graph and time-series: each is built for a different kind of question.

slides.title: Write the access patterns first
slides.tldr: On one page, list what the app will do with data, how often, and with what guarantees. The database name falls out of it.

slides.title: When in doubt, go relational
slides.tldr: Most business data is linked, so the default is PostgreSQL or MySQL; the shapeless part can go in a JSON column.

slides.title: A second database: when, and at what price
slides.tldr: Every new database means new backups, monitoring and syncing work; keep the truth in one place and make the rest copies of it.

slides.title: The same order in six shapes
slides.tldr: One order looks different in each database family; the shape decides which questions are one line and which are impossible.

slides.title: One fact, three places, three versions
slides.tldr: Write the same fact in several places and one day the copies drift apart; then nobody can say which one is right.

slides.title: Normalization: one home for every fact
slides.tldr: Normalization means storing each fact once, in its own table; everything else holds only its ID (a foreign key).

slides.title: Constraints: the database as a guard
slides.tldr: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY and CHECK stop bad data from entering inside the database itself, even when the code gets it wrong.

slides.title: When copying is right, and when it is not
slides.tldr: Copy a snapshot of facts that change over time but must stay fixed in history (price, address); normalize the rest.

slides.title: Millions of rows, all read every time
slides.tldr: With no index, the database reads every row of the table for each query; 10 thousand rows go unnoticed, 2 million do not.

slides.title: What a B-tree index really is
slides.tldr: A B-tree is a sorted tree: from the root, three or four steps down reach any value, and because neighbors sit together, ranges and ORDER BY are cheap too.

slides.title: Composite index: column order
slides.tldr: Column order in a composite index decides which queries it helps: equality columns first, range or sort columns after, and a condition must start from the left or the index is useless.

slides.title: Reading a query plan with EXPLAIN
slides.tldr: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) shows how the database really ran the query; Seq Scan turning into Index Scan means the index works, and a covering index even skips the table rows.

slides.title: The price of indexes: writes get slower
slides.tldr: Every index speeds up reads but must also be updated on every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE; keep only the useful ones, and use partial indexes to keep them small.

segments.title: Under the hood: B-tree vs LSM

slides.title: Same SQL, a different engine inside
slides.tldr: The storage engine inside a database decides which jobs are fast and which are slow, so one engine is not equally good for write-heavy and read-heavy work.

slides.title: B-tree versus LSM-tree
slides.tldr: A B-tree finds the right spot at write time, so reads are good; an LSM-tree collects writes first and sorts later, so writes are good.

slides.title: WAL, memtable, SSTable and compaction
slides.tldr: A write goes first to the WAL (safety), then to memory (speed), and to a disk file when memory fills; later compaction merges files and clears old and duplicate data.

slides.title: Which database uses which engine, and when
slides.tldr: PostgreSQL and MySQL (InnoDB) are B-tree based; Cassandra, ScyllaDB and RocksDB are LSM based. For ordinary business apps, B-tree is the default.

slides.title: Turning off durability because it feels slow
slides.tldr: Turning off fsync makes writes fast but a crash can corrupt the whole database; for data you can afford to lose, switch off synchronous_commit inside a single transaction instead.

slides.title: Slow INSERTs: batch before you tune
slides.tldr: Every commit waits for one disk flush. 1,000 single-row commits wait 1,000 times; one transaction of 1,000 rows waits once, and risks nothing.

segments.title: Generating IDs: UUID, ULID, Snowflake, sequences

slides.title: IDs like take-a-number tickets: simple, but limited
slides.tldr: Auto-increment IDs are simple and small, but they can be guessed, they leak the size of your business, and they collide when several databases or servers generate them.

slides.title: Five kinds of ID side by side
slides.tldr: Sequence, UUIDv4, UUIDv7, ULID and Snowflake differ on four questions: size, sortable by time, guessability, and whether they need coordination.

slides.title: Why random IDs tire out the index
slides.tldr: A primary key lives in a B-tree. A random UUIDv4 writes to any leaf of the tree each time (pages split, caches miss); a time-sorted ID is appended to the last leaf.

slides.title: Using UUIDv7 with Symfony Uid
slides.tldr: With the Symfony Uid component, create `Uuid::v7()` in the constructor, give Doctrine a `UuidType`, and put `Requirement::UUID_V7` on the route; the ID is known before flush.

slides.title: A hard-to-guess ID is not security
slides.tldr: Even when IDs are hard to guess, you cannot skip authorization; and a UUIDv7 reveals when it was created, so think about that if the time must stay secret.

slides.title: The danger of a single copy
slides.tldr: When the only database server dies, everything stops, and one machine carries all the read load. Replication keeps several copies: one leader takes the writes and the followers receive copies.

slides.title: Sync versus async replication
slides.tldr: With async, the leader says "done" without waiting for followers: fast, but a crash can lose the latest writes. With sync, it waits: safer, but slower.

slides.title: Lag: you can't see your own write
slides.tldr: An async follower runs a little behind (replication lag). Read from a follower right after a write and the user doesn't see their own new data; this problem is called read-your-own-writes.

slides.title: A primary/replica setup in Doctrine
slides.tldr: With replicas in doctrine.yaml, DoctrineBundle sends reads to a replica and writes to the primary; after a write, every read in that request goes to the primary on its own, and a sticky listener handles the rest.

slides.title: Failover and split brain
slides.tldr: When the leader dies, a follower must be promoted to leader (failover); but if the old leader comes back alive and both take writes, you get split brain and the data divides in two.

slides.title: Sharding is the last resort, not the first
slides.tldr: Sharding splits data across several servers. It adds huge complexity, so exhaust indexes, caching, a bigger server, replicas and partitioning first.

slides.title: The shard key and the router
slides.tldr: Every row has a shard key. A router computes which shard the row lives on, and the app talks straight to that shard.

slides.title: The wrong key: one shard takes all the load
slides.tldr: A good shard key spreads load evenly, appears in most queries and never changes. A bad one (country, date) piles everything on one hot shard.

slides.title: In code: partitions and a shard router
slides.tldr: Start with PostgreSQL declarative partitions on one server. For real sharding, give Doctrine one connection per shard and a router built on virtual buckets.

slides.title: Adding a shard: move 20%, not 80%
slides.tldr: Going from 4 to 5 shards with hash % N moves 80% of the rows. With 1024 buckets you reassign about 205 buckets (20%), one at a time, while the app runs.

slides.title: Cross-shard queries and resharding
slides.tldr: A query without the shard key fans out to every shard (scatter-gather) and is slow. Joins and transactions across shards are hard, and resharding is painful, so plan ahead.

segments.title: Consistency models: who sees what, when

slides.title: Refresh the page, travel back in time
slides.tldr: With several copies of the data, not everyone sees the same thing at the same moment. The rules for who sees what, and when, are called a consistency model.

slides.title: From strong to eventual: a ladder of rules
slides.tldr: Strong consistency always shows the latest data but is slower and less available. Eventual is the fastest but may show stale data for a while. A few handy rules sit in between.

slides.title: Seeing your own writes, and time moving forward
slides.tldr: Read-your-writes and monotonic reads are cheap to get: after a write, read from the primary when needed, and always send each user to the same replica.

slides.title: Causal: the question before the answer
slides.tldr: When events depend on each other (a question and its answer), breaking their order makes users see nonsense. Causal consistency keeps it: the answer points to its cause, and a read waits for that cause.

slides.title: A different rule for each feature
slides.tldr: Demanding strong everywhere is slow and fragile; eventual everywhere is dangerous for money. For each feature, pick the loosest rule that doesn't confuse the user.

slides.title: 51 queries on one page
slides.tldr: One query for the list, then one more per row: that is N+1. The code looks fine, yet the page slows down as the data grows.

slides.title: Why Doctrine runs queries silently
slides.tldr: Doctrine puts an empty proxy where a related entity should be, and the first touch fires a query. Count the queries per request and N+1 shows up.

slides.title: One query: fetch join and DTO
slides.tldr: Load to-one relations in the same query with a fetch join. For read-only lists, skip entities and build a DTO from just the columns you need.

slides.title: Batch loading for collections
slides.tldr: Joining a to-many collection multiplies the rows. Instead, run a second query with `IN (…)` that loads all the collections at once: 2 queries in total.

slides.title: LIMIT with a JOIN: why does the page have fewer orders?
slides.tldr: With a collection fetch join, `setMaxResults(20)` applies to SQL rows, not orders. You get 5 orders instead of 20.

slides.title: The monthly report started, and checkout froze
slides.tldr: Run fast little transactions and heavy reports on the same database and the report eats every resource, so customers' orders slow down.

slides.title: OLTP vs OLAP, and derived data
slides.tldr: OLTP is for small, fast reads and writes; OLAP is for big calculations. A separate copy built from the original data (the source of truth) is derived data.

slides.title: Precompute summaries with a materialized view
slides.tldr: Compute the heavy query's result once and keep it like a table. Reports read the ready-made result, and the Scheduler refreshes it. The refresh itself still runs on the primary.

slides.title: A view answers only the question it was built for
slides.tldr: A refresh recomputes everything on the primary, and a view serves one fixed question. A small daily summary table is cheaper to refresh and rolls up; changing questions need a warehouse.

slides.title: Change data capture: let the changes travel on their own
slides.tldr: If the app writes to two places by hand, one write will eventually be missed. CDC reads the database's own log and sends the changes on, at the price of extra infrastructure and a log to watch.

slides.title: Photos in the database, photos on the server disk
slides.tldr: Photos in the database bloat it. Photos on the server's disk go missing on a second server and vanish on deploy.

slides.title: Object storage: the database keeps only the key
slides.tldr: Files go to object storage; the database keeps the file's key and metadata. Write through Flysystem and the code survives a change of storage.

slides.title: Presigned URLs: send the file straight to storage
slides.tldr: The server mints a time-limited signed form; the Vue app POSTs the file straight to storage, with a size cap the storage itself enforces. The file never passes through your server.

slides.title: Confirm or clean up: no upload left behind
slides.tldr: A client can fetch a URL and never upload, or upload and vanish before confirming. Record every upload as pending, promote it only after the server's own check, and delete whatever stays pending.

slides.title: Large files: in pieces, and resumable
slides.tldr: Send a big file in one go and a dropped connection means starting over. Multipart upload splits it into parts, and only the failed part is resent.

slides.title: Resume after a crash: ask storage what it already has
slides.tldr: Storage remembers every stored part of an open upload. After a crash or a refresh, ask it with ListParts and send only the missing parts.

slides.title: One renamed field broke the mobile app
slides.tldr: Change the shape (schema) of an API or message and every reader that expects the old shape breaks. Both sides never deploy at the same moment, so changes must be made carefully.

slides.title: JSON, Protobuf, Avro: how each one writes data
slides.tldr: JSON is human-readable but bulky; Protobuf and Avro are compact and schema-driven. Protobuf identifies fields by number, while Avro carries the writer's schema alongside.

slides.title: Safe changes: adding, removing and renaming fields
slides.tldr: Add new fields as optional or with a default. Stop using a field before you remove it. A rename is an add, then a later remove of the old one.

slides.title: The trap of reused numbers and required fields
slides.tldr: Reuse the number or name of a removed field and old data gets read with the wrong meaning. Use reserved to forbid it.

slides.title: Schema registry: the guardian of changes
slides.tldr: A schema registry stores every schema version, checks compatibility before a new schema is accepted, and messages carry only a schema id.

slides.title: One ALTER TABLE froze the whole site
slides.tldr: A schema-change command on a big table holds a lock while every query behind it queues up. New code running against an old schema breaks things too.

slides.title: Expand, migrate, contract: build the bridge alongside
slides.tldr: Three safe steps: first add the new structure (expand), then move data and code over (migrate), and finally remove the old one (contract). Each step is its own deploy.

slides.title: The expand step in a Doctrine Migration
slides.tldr: Write Doctrine Migrations with a nullable column, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `lock_timeout`. Locks stay short, and a failure backs out quickly.

slides.title: Backfill: millions of rows in small batches
slides.tldr: One `UPDATE` over 10 million rows means a long lock and a huge transaction. Instead, run a re-runnable command that handles 1,000 rows at a time with a short pause.

slides.title: Traps: NOT NULL, foreign keys and plain indexes
slides.tldr: On a big table, a direct `SET NOT NULL`, `ADD FOREIGN KEY` or plain `CREATE INDEX` scans or locks the whole table. Doing it in two steps (NOT VALID, then VALIDATE) is safe.

slides.title: The price changed, and so did the old invoices
slides.tldr: UPDATE wipes out the old value, so you can't answer "what was it before?", "who changed it?" or "which price applied then?".

slides.title: Audit history: who changed what, and when
slides.tldr: Every important change adds a new row to an audit table: who, when, which record, the old and new values. Rows are never changed or deleted.

slides.title: Effective dating: which price on which date
slides.tldr: Each price row has `valid_from` and `valid_to`. One query answers "what was the price on 10 February?", and an exclusion constraint prevents overlapping periods.

slides.title: Soft delete: the convenience and the traps
slides.tldr: Soft delete means setting `deleted_at`. But unique constraints get in the way, and forgetting the filter in one query shows deleted data. The fixes are a partial unique index and a Doctrine filter.

slides.title: "Delete my data" and the hidden copies
slides.tldr: A user's data isn't only in the users table: copies live in logs, backups, search, analytics and caches. Skip lifecycle planning and deletion becomes nearly impossible.

slides.title: Retention policy and data minimization
slides.tldr: For each kind of data, write down in advance why you keep it, for how long, and what happens afterwards. And collect only what you truly need from the start.

slides.title: Purge jobs and archives: deleting by the rules
slides.tldr: Delete expired data nightly through the Scheduler, in small batches. For data you occasionally need, archive it to cheap storage first, verify, then delete.

slides.title: Erasure: delete, anonymize, and tell the copies
slides.tldr: For an account-deletion request, anonymize personal data while keeping legal records, tell every copy with an event, and keep an erasure list for backups.

slides.title: Last month's sales: three departments, three numbers
slides.tldr: When everyone copies the data and does their own sums, one question gets three answers. A data platform means one place, one definition, one set of rules.

slides.title: Warehouse, lake, lakehouse: three kinds of storehouse
slides.tldr: A warehouse is a tidy store of clean data; a lake is a huge reservoir of raw data of every kind; a lakehouse tries to bring the strengths of both into one place.

slides.title: The ELT pipeline: bring it in first, cook in the warehouse
slides.tldr: With ELT, raw data goes into the warehouse first (Extract, Load), then SQL cleans and shapes it there (Transform). Symfony extracts to a file in the lake and the warehouse loads that file into the raw layer.

slides.title: Transform: clean and define inside the warehouse
slides.tldr: Staging removes duplicates by keeping the newest row per id. The mart settles the business definition once, in SQL, so every dashboard reads the same number.

slides.title: Batch or streaming: how fast do you need it?
slides.tldr: Batch moves data in one go at set times: simple and cheap. Streaming moves every event immediately: fast but complex. How much delay you can tolerate decides it.

slides.title: Governance: owners, quality and a catalog
slides.tldr: Every dataset gets an owner, a written definition and quality checks, plus a catalog everyone can search. That settles "which number do I trust?".

topics.title: Search & Caching
topics.summary: Finding things fast and never doing the same work twice, from search indexes to cache stampedes.

slides.title: LIKE search: fine on small data, breaks on big data
slides.tldr: LIKE %x% reads every row, ignores typos, and has no idea which result fits best.

slides.title: Inverted index: from a word to its documents
slides.tldr: An inverted index lists, for every word, the documents that contain it; searching is just fetching that list.

slides.title: Analyzer: the factory that turns text into terms
slides.tldr: An analyzer splits text into words, lowercases them and reduces them to their root; if index and query don't use the same analyzer, words won't match.

slides.title: Relevance: which result comes first
slides.tldr: A search engine gives every document a score (BM25): higher for rare words, for repeated words, and for matches in short text.

slides.title: Searching from Symfony: results and facets in one request
slides.tldr: A facet is a counted list like "Samsung (12), Apple (8)" beside the results; send the query, filter and aggregation in one request.

slides.title: Elasticsearch / OpenSearch: when to bring one in, when not to
slides.tldr: A search engine is powerful, but you must run a separate cluster, keep data in sync and accept a delay of a second or two; for small data, database full-text is enough.

segments.title: Keeping a search index up to date

slides.title: In the database, missing from search
slides.tldr: Write to the database and the search index separately from a controller and one failure leaves them disagreeing; this trap is called a dual write.

slides.title: The database is the original, the index is its copy, with a pipeline in between
slides.tldr: Write to the database first, then put a message with just the ID on a queue; a worker reads the fresh state from the database and updates the index.

slides.title: The write side: flush, then one small message
slides.tldr: The write code only flushes to the database and dispatches an IndexProduct message; the message goes to its own transport, with retries.

slides.title: The read side: a handler that is safe to run again and again
slides.tldr: The handler reads the product from the database: PUT it under its own ID if it exists, DELETE if not, and throw on failure so Messenger retries.

slides.title: The gap of a few seconds: eventual consistency
slides.tldr: There will always be a gap of a second or two between a database write and its appearing in search; serve the page right after a write, and every decision, from the database.

slides.title: Rebuilding the whole index with zero downtime
slides.tldr: Build a new index and fill it from the database in batches, then flip an alias in one step; the app always knows the alias, never the real index.

slides.title: The same calculation, 50,000 times a day
slides.tldr: Recomputing an answer that barely changes on every request wastes time and servers; a cache keeps that answer on hand.

slides.title: Cache-aside: the app looks, and the app fills
slides.tldr: In cache-aside the app checks the cache first; on a miss it fetches from the database and stores the result itself. It is the most common strategy.

slides.title: Cache-aside in Symfony: a single get() call
slides.tldr: Symfony Cache contracts' get(key, callback) looks up, runs the callback on a miss and stores the result; plug in Redis as the backend.

slides.title: Three more strategies for reads and writes
slides.tldr: In read-through, write-through and write-behind the cache itself talks to the database; they differ in when a write reaches the database and where the risk sits.

slides.title: What not to cache, and one terrible mistake
slides.tldr: Caching per-user data under a shared key lets one person see another's data; caching accuracy-critical data like money and stock is risky too.

slides.title: Which strategy, and when
slides.tldr: For most Symfony apps cache-aside is enough; use write-through when you need fresh values, and write-behind only for load-absorbing writes where loss is acceptable.

slides.title: The price changed, the board still shows the old one
slides.tldr: A cached answer is a copy of the real data; when the original changes, the copy doesn't follow, so users see stale data. This problem is called cache invalidation.

slides.title: TTL: every piece of data gets an expiry
slides.tldr: TTL is the lifetime of a cached answer; when it runs out the entry vanishes. Set it by how stale the data may get, and treat TTL as the last line of defense.

slides.title: Cache keys: the right key, and a version
slides.tldr: The key must contain everything that changes the answer: ID, language, page. A version in the key lets you void all entries of an old shape at once.

slides.title: Deleting many entries at once with tags
slides.tldr: One product lives in many cache entries; tag them all, and after a product change a single invalidateTags() call removes every one.

slides.title: When to delete, and in what order
slides.tldr: Write to the database and commit first, then delete from the cache. The other way around lets one request put the old value back in the cache; so keep a TTL too.

slides.title: The entry expired, and a thousand people rushed in
slides.tldr: When a popular cache entry expires, a thousand requests miss at once and all send the same heavy query to the database; this storm is called a cache stampede.

slides.title: One person cooks, the rest wait
slides.tldr: The core of stopping a stampede: for one key only one request rebuilds the value at a time (a lock), and the rest wait or show the stale value.

slides.title: Spread out the expiry: jitter and early expiration
slides.tldr: Adding a random few seconds to the expiry (jitter) stops many entries dying together; and Symfony's beta parameter lets one request rebuild the value slightly before it expires.

slides.title: Show the stale one, build the new one behind
slides.tldr: Give an entry a soft expiry and a hard expiry; once the soft one passes, one request takes a lock and rebuilds, while the rest get the old value.

slides.title: The lock itself can become a new danger
slides.tldr: A lock without an expiry, or waiting forever, leaves everyone stuck if the holder dies and runs the PHP workers out; give the lock a TTL and put a limit on waiting.

slides.title: Downloading the same file every time
slides.tldr: Without Cache-Control, the browser and the CDN don't know what to keep, so the same JS, images and API answers come from the origin server on every visit. HTTP caching stops this waste.

slides.title: Cache-Control: who keeps it, and for how long
slides.tldr: The Cache-Control header says who (the browser or the CDN) may keep an answer and for how long: max-age, s-maxage, public, private, no-cache, no-store, stale-while-revalidate.

slides.title: ETag: has it changed? No, so no download
slides.tldr: An ETag is the fingerprint of an answer. The browser sends it back in If-None-Match; if it matches, the server replies 304 with no body and the browser uses its own copy.

slides.title: Headers and 304 in Symfony
slides.tldr: Use the #[Cache] attribute to set max-age, public and stale-while-revalidate; build an ETag and call response->isNotModified() to return 304 before any heavy work.

slides.title: CDN, cache keys and cache busting
slides.tldr: A CDN builds its cache key from the URL (and any Vary headers); a hash in the file name plus a one-year immutable lifetime means a new deploy bypasses the old file's cache by itself.

slides.title: The wrong public: one person's page for everyone
slides.tldr: Putting public or s-maxage on a personal or cookie-dependent answer lets the CDN serve one user's page to others; that is a direct data leak.

topics.title: Rules, Config & Feature Flags
topics.summary: Changing behavior without changing code: feature flags, configuration, and where business rules belong.

slides.title: A bad release at 11 pm, and no switch to undo it
slides.tldr: Deploying code and opening a feature to users are two separate jobs. A feature flag splits them, so a bad release can be switched off without a deploy.

slides.title: Four kinds of flags: different jobs, different lifespans
slides.tldr: Flags come in four kinds: release (open a feature slowly), ops/kill switch (emergency off), experiment (A/B) and permission (who gets it). The kind decides the lifespan and the owner.

slides.title: A simple flag service and percentage rollout in Symfony
slides.tldr: Keep flag state in the database and cache it with a short TTL. For a percentage rollout, hash the user id into 0–99 so the same user always gets the same result.

slides.title: Flags in Vue: the server decides, the client displays
slides.tldr: Make the flag decision on the server and send the per-user result to Vue through an API. Vue only shows or hides; enforcement stays on the server.

slides.title: Hiding the button is not a lock: guard the API too
slides.tldr: A hidden button is still a reachable URL. Check the same flag inside the API action and answer 404 while it is off.

slides.title: Flag debt: the switch nobody flips
slides.tldr: Old release flags that were never deleted keep two code paths alive, double your tests and create places people are afraid to touch. Give every flag an owner and a removal date.

slides.title: It works on my machine, but not in prod
slides.tldr: Addresses, passwords and settings hardcoded in the code are right in one environment and wrong in another, and a password that reaches git is leaked for good. Keep config outside the code.

slides.title: Build once, run everywhere
slides.tldr: The 12-factor rule: the same build or image runs in every environment, and the differences come from environment variables. What you tested on staging is exactly what ships to prod.

slides.title: Using env variables in Symfony
slides.tldr: Put safe defaults in .env and the real values on the server. In code, inject them with types via #[Autowire(env: 'int:NAME')], and in YAML write %env(int:NAME)%.

slides.title: Config and secrets are not the same thing
slides.tldr: Leaking an address or a timeout does little harm; leaking a password or an API key does. Keep secret values in the Symfony secrets vault or a secret manager, never in git.

slides.title: When environments drift apart: config drift
slides.tldr: If code changes behavior by checking APP_ENV, or environments slowly move apart, then tests on staging no longer show how prod behaves. Put the differences in config, not in code branches.

segments.title: Business rules: in code or in data?

slides.title: Discount rules that change every week
slides.tldr: When the business team changes a rule once a week, waiting for a developer and a deploy each time is slow and irritating. That raises the question of moving such rules into data.

slides.title: Should a rule live in code or in data?
slides.tldr: Decide with four questions: how often it changes, who changes it, what a mistake costs, and how complex it is. Simple, frequently changed rules with a capped downside go in data; complex or risky ones stay in code.

slides.title: Running rules with Symfony ExpressionLanguage
slides.tldr: Store each rule's condition as a string in the database and let ExpressionLanguage evaluate it. Pass only a small facts DTO, and check each rule with lint() when you save it.

slides.title: Versioning, testing and dry-running rules
slides.tldr: Rules kept in data must go through versioning, tests and approval, just like code: a new version, tests, a dry run on old orders, a start date, and the old versions kept.

slides.title: The price of getting rules-as-data wrong
slides.tldr: Unguarded rules can turn a single typo into a 100% discount, and complex rules in data become an untested programming language. Keep the ceiling in code.

topics.title: Transactions & Concurrency
topics.summary: What happens when two people change the same thing at once, and how to keep money, tickets and stock safe.

segments.title: ACID: four promises of a transaction

slides.title: The money left, but never arrived
slides.tldr: If the two steps of one job are saved separately, a single error in between makes the money vanish.

slides.title: ACID: the four promises of a transaction
slides.tldr: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: all or nothing, rules stay intact, half-done work stays hidden, committed means committed.

slides.title: Transactions in Doctrine: flush() and wrapInTransaction()
slides.tldr: flush() is already a transaction; when a job has several steps, locks or raw SQL, wrap the whole job in wrapInTransaction().

slides.title: Rollback can't take back an email or an SMS
slides.tldr: A transaction only undoes changes in its own database; an SMS, email or HTTP call made inside it stays sent and also holds locks.

slides.title: What a transaction protects, and what it doesn't
slides.tldr: A transaction stops half-done work and rule violations; it does not stop race conditions, outside services or wrong calculations.

slides.title: One transaction, two queries, two different truths
slides.tldr: Even inside one transaction, another commit can slip in between two queries; the isolation level decides how much gets in.

slides.title: Three read problems: dirty, non-repeatable, phantom
slides.tldr: Dirty read = reading unconfirmed writes; non-repeatable = a row you read changes; phantom = new rows appear.

slides.title: Two write problems: lost update and write skew
slides.tldr: In a lost update, a write to the same row disappears; in write skew, two valid writes to different rows together break a rule.

slides.title: The four levels: which one stops which problem
slides.tldr: Read uncommitted → read committed → repeatable read → serializable: the higher you go, the fewer anomalies, but the more waiting and aborted transactions.

slides.title: When to raise the level, and why you must retry
slides.tldr: Keep the default level; when a rule spans several rows, make just that one transaction SERIALIZABLE and retry on serialization failure.

slides.title: Two phones, one balance, spent twice
slides.tldr: When two requests read the same stale balance at once, both pass the check, and money that doesn't exist gets spent.

slides.title: Where the gap is: check-then-act and read-modify-write
slides.tldr: Nearly every race condition has the same shape: read something, think, then write, and someone else can get in between the read and the write.

slides.title: How to catch a race condition in your own code
slides.tldr: Be suspicious of any read-then-write in code, then fire 20 identical requests at once and check the result.

slides.title: The "check if it exists first" trap, and its fix
slides.tldr: Searching before inserting a new row races; the real guard is the database's unique constraint, and you handle its exception.

slides.title: Pessimistic lock: take the key, everyone else queues
slides.tldr: SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the row as you read it; the second request waits in line and then reads the correct balance.

slides.title: PESSIMISTIC_WRITE in Doctrine: rules and time limits
slides.tldr: Pass PESSIMISTIC_WRITE to find() inside an open transaction, keep the work short, and put a cap on the waiting time.

slides.title: Optimistic lock: don't hold anything, check the seal on the way out
slides.tldr: Keep a version column on the row; the UPDATE applies only if the version is still what it was; otherwise the conflict is caught.

slides.title: Which lock? One rule to choose
slides.tldr: Rare collisions and slow humans: optimistic. Frequent collisions and quick code: pessimistic. A plain counter needs neither: one atomic UPDATE does it.

slides.title: Advisory locks and Symfony Lock: a lock with no row
slides.tldr: You can lock a name instead of a row. It suits cron jobs, exports and multi-server work, but the TTL has a trap.

slides.title: Deadlock: each waiting for the other
slides.tldr: When two transactions take locks in opposite order, both get stuck; always lock in the same order, and retry when a deadlock error occurs.

slides.title: The last phone, sold to two people
slides.tldr: Put the condition and the change in one SQL statement and the database closes the gap itself: UPDATE … WHERE stock >= n, then check how many rows changed.

slides.title: Atomic UPDATE in Symfony: DQL and DBAL
slides.tldr: Instead of getter and setter, run `SET stock = stock - :n WHERE … AND stock >= :n` through DQL or DBAL; a result of 0 means no stock.

slides.title: Compare-and-swap: "is it still in the state I expect?"
slides.tldr: Put the old state in the UPDATE's WHERE (status = 'pending'); affected rows 1 means you won, 0 means someone else got there first.

slides.title: Unique constraints and upsert: keep the rule in the database
slides.tldr: Write the uniqueness rule as an index and the database blocks duplicates itself; upsert does "create if missing, update if present" in one statement.

slides.title: Atomic doesn't help if you ignore the result
slides.tldr: If you run an atomic UPDATE and never look at affected rows, the code assumes it always won and completes the order even on 0.

slides.title: The 10 minutes of payment: whose seat is it?
slides.tldr: If you don't hold the seat before payment, people pay and then hear "sold out"; if you hold it with no release, it stays blocked forever. The fix: a hold with a time limit.

slides.title: The life of a hold: four states
slides.tldr: Every hold is a record: from held it becomes either confirmed, or expired or canceled. The expiry lives in the record's expires_at column.

slides.title: Building a hold: a unique index and an expiring row
slides.tldr: Put a partial unique index on active holds; expire stale ones before creating a new hold; if the unique rule fires, the seat is taken.

slides.title: Confirm and clean up: expiry is the truth, cleanup is just sweeping
slides.tldr: When confirming, verify that expires_at is still in the future; the cleanup job only keeps things tidy, and correctness doesn't depend on it.

slides.title: Payment arrives after the expiry: now what?
slides.tldr: When payment is slow, the money can arrive after the hold ran out; if the seat has gone to someone else, that payment must be refunded, never quietly confirmed.

slides.title: Saved in the database, but nobody was told
slides.tldr: When you write to the database and then to another system (a queue, email, another service), a failure in between leaves one done and the other not. This is the dual-write problem.

slides.title: Two-phase commit: getting everyone's "yes", and why it is avoided
slides.tldr: In 2PC, a coordinator first asks everyone "ready?" and commits only if all say yes; but if the coordinator dies, everyone is left stuck.

slides.title: Outbox: write the notification in the same transaction
slides.tldr: Write the notification into an outbox table in the same transaction as the order; a separate relay sends it to the queue later. The notification can't get lost.

slides.title: Saga: every step has an "undo step"
slides.tldr: Break a job spanning many services into small steps; if a step fails, undo the earlier successful steps in reverse order with compensations.

slides.title: Starting the undo steps, and what if an undo fails
slides.tldr: An orchestrator records each finished step; on a failure it undoes them last to first, one message at a time. A failed undo is retried until it works, so every undo must be safe to repeat.

slides.title: Arrives twice, runs once: the idempotent consumer
slides.tldr: An outbox, retries and the broker can all deliver the same message more than once. A consumer that remembers each message id and does nothing the second time is safe.

topics.title: Queues, Events & Background Work
topics.summary: Not every job belongs inside the request. Queues, events and workers let you do it later, safely.

segments.title: Events vs commands, queues vs streams

slides.title: One button, six and a half seconds of waiting
slides.tldr: Send the email, SMS, PDF and courier call inside the order request and the customer waits, and one failure breaks everything.

slides.title: A command says "do this", an event says "this happened"
slides.tldr: A command orders one specific handler to do a job. An event only announces what happened, and zero or many listeners react on their own.

slides.title: Symfony Messenger: message, handler, transport, worker
slides.tldr: A message is a small DTO, the handler does the job, the transport stores the message, and a worker in a separate process picks it up and runs the handler.

slides.title: Queue vs stream: the order spike and the ledger
slides.tldr: A queue gives each message to one worker and deletes it when done. A stream keeps every message in order, and each reader reads from its own position.

slides.title: The trap: in the queue does not mean done
slides.tldr: dispatch() means the job was written down, not done. Make async an answer the user needs right now and you have to lie to them.

slides.title: Two confirmation emails for one order
slides.tldr: If a worker finishes the job but dies before sending the ack, the broker delivers the message again and the job runs twice.

slides.title: At-most-once, at-least-once and "exactly-once"
slides.tldr: Ack before the work and a message can be lost; ack after and it can arrive twice. Exactly-once is really at-least-once plus an idempotent handler.

slides.title: Ordering and partitions: same key, same line
slides.tldr: With many workers running at once, message order breaks. Send messages with the same key to the same partition and the order holds within that key.

slides.title: Handling ack, duplicates and order in Messenger
slides.tldr: Messenger acks only after the handler succeeds, so delivery is at-least-once. Skip repeats by message id, and set a group id only where order matters.

slides.title: "Apply only if newer" is for snapshots, not changes
slides.tldr: A version check drops late messages. That is right when a message carries the whole new state, and silently loses money when it carries only a change.

slides.title: The message that never succeeds
slides.tldr: Rerun a broken message again and again in a rush and a failing API takes even more pressure while the queue clogs up. You need a rule for cutting it off.

slides.title: Retry with backoff, and the DLQ at the end
slides.tldr: Retry a limited number of times, waiting twice as long each time. If it still fails, park the message in a dead-letter queue and let a human look.

slides.title: Retry strategy and failure transport in Messenger
slides.tldr: Set retry_strategy and failure_transport on the transport. Throw a plain exception for temporary failures and UnrecoverableMessageHandlingException for permanent ones.

slides.title: The trap: work done twice after a retry
slides.tldr: Retries and redeliveries mean a handler can run more than once. Record the message id in a processed-message table so the work happens only once.

slides.title: The 2 a.m. report and a server restart halfway
slides.tldr: Run one huge job in a single go and a mid-run crash means starting over. Run cron on two servers and the job runs twice.

slides.title: Visibility timeout and priority
slides.tldr: When a worker takes a message it is hidden for a while, and if no ack arrives in time another worker gets it. Urgent work in its own queue never waits behind slow work.

slides.title: Symfony Scheduler and priority transports
slides.tldr: Instead of cron, keep the schedule in code, use a lock so it runs on only one server, and give urgent work its own transport.

slides.title: The trap: one giant job in a single go
slides.tldr: Split big work into small chunks. Each chunk is one message, and the next chunk's message carries a checkpoint (the last id), so a crash reruns only the current chunk.

slides.title: Seeing your jobs: what to measure
slides.tldr: Background jobs die quietly. Measure queue depth, the age of the oldest message, the failure rate and the run time, and set alerts on them.

slides.title: Two more servers, and old code keeps running
slides.tldr: Extra workers on extra servers share one queue for free. But the deploy that restarts them signals through a local cache, so only one server hears it.

slides.title: One shared place for the stop signal
slides.tldr: The stop command leaves a mark in the app cache and workers read it. Put the cache where every server can see it, or restart per server, or replace containers.

slides.title: Keeping workers alive, and how many to run
slides.tldr: Work out the worker count from jobs per second and job time, then let a supervisor run that many and restart them. The flags make each worker retire cleanly.

slides.title: The trap: state that lives on one server
slides.tldr: A file on one server's disk or a value cached in a worker's memory breaks on many servers. Send IDs, keep files in shared storage, cache with a TTL.

slides.title: When the transport or the database is the limit
slides.tldr: Watch queue depth and message age to know when to add workers. Each worker costs a database connection, and the transport must keep up, so choose it by volume.

slides.title: Five SMS for one order, and the one that mattered never arrived
slides.tldr: Blast every event to every channel and users get fed up and opt out. Then when a provider breaks, the urgent message is the one that gets lost.

slides.title: The notification pipeline: preferences, dedup, provider
slides.tldr: An event doesn't go straight to SMS. First the user's preferences, then dedup and throttling, and finally the provider, with a failover if one breaks.

slides.title: Symfony Notifier: channels, preferences and failover
slides.tldr: Build a Notification in Notifier, take the channels from the user's preferences, and add a backup provider with failover(...) in the transport DSN.

slides.title: The OTP must get through: transactional vs marketing
slides.tldr: If every message obeys preferences, a user who switched notifications off never gets the login code. Mark messages transactional or not, and let only transactional ones skip preferences.

slides.title: The same message once, and a digest when there are too many
slides.tldr: Retries and redeliveries send a message twice, so stop that with a dedup key. Past the limit, ordinary messages are held back by a rate limiter and collected in a digest.

slides.title: Emptying the digest: a scheduled job
slides.tldr: A digest helps only if something sends it. A Scheduler task gathers each user's waiting items every hour, sends one message, and clears them only after the send worked.

topics.title: Time
topics.summary: Clocks lie. The mistakes everyone makes with timestamps, time zones, DST and timeouts.

slides.title: The courier API answered in −2.7 seconds
slides.tldr: If the server clock is set back midway, "end − start" comes out negative. The assumption that a clock only moves forward is wrong.

slides.title: Four ways a clock lies
slides.tldr: Skew, drift, NTP jumps and leap seconds: for these four reasons two machines' clocks never match exactly, and even a single clock doesn't run in a straight line.

slides.title: The wall clock vs the stopwatch
slides.tldr: A wall clock tells you what time it is and can jump. A monotonic clock only moves forward and tells you how long something took. Always use the second one to measure time.

slides.title: Symfony Clock: handing time to your tests
slides.tldr: Instead of calling new DateTimeImmutable() directly, inject a ClockInterface. In tests, use MockClock to freeze time and move it forward as you like.

slides.title: Ordering events by comparing two servers' timestamps
slides.tldr: If server A's clock runs 80 ms ahead, a cancel that happens later gets a smaller timestamp than the create that happened earlier. For ordering, you need numbers, not timestamps.

slides.title: The newer edit vanished
slides.tldr: If you pick the "latest" write by comparing two machines' clock times, the stale write from the clock that runs ahead wins, and the genuinely newer write is silently lost.

slides.title: Logical clocks: counting cause and effect, not time
slides.tldr: Each machine keeps its own counter. It travels with every message, and on receipt the receiver sets its counter to max(own, received) + 1. So causes come first and effects after.

slides.title: Ordering work: version numbers and sequences
slides.tldr: Give every entity its own version number and increment it atomically with each change. Drop any event whose version is smaller than what you already have. No clock needed.

slides.title: Four ways to order events, and when to use each
slides.tldr: Clocks are approximate; Lamport gives cause and effect; version numbers create order in one place; a hybrid logical clock reads like a clock and also respects cause and effect.

slides.title: How to get rid of last-write-wins
slides.tldr: Choosing the "newer" write by the client's updatedAt lets stale writes overwrite newer ones. Detect conflicts by comparing versions, and merge fields one at a time.

slides.title: The meeting suddenly moved by an hour
slides.tldr: Store a London user's "every Monday at 10 am" meeting in UTC and it slides to 11 am after the DST change, with no bug in the code.

slides.title: Two kinds of time: the instant and the wall clock
slides.tldr: Store a moment that has happened in UTC. Store a future local event as the local time plus the zone name (Europe/London), not as an offset.

slides.title: The DST gap and the doubled hour
slides.tldr: In spring one hour of local time doesn't exist (a gap); in autumn one hour happens twice (an overlap). Put an event in that time and the code quietly guesses; detect both cases and decide on purpose.

slides.title: Storing and computing: SQL and PHP
slides.tldr: Past moments go in timestamptz. Future events get the local time plus the zone name, and a separately computed next_run_at (UTC) for the scheduler.

slides.title: Displaying: in the user's zone, in Vue
slides.tldr: The API sends UTC (ISO 8601, ending in Z); in Vue, Intl.DateTimeFormat formats it in the user's own zone. For an event elsewhere, show the event's own zone too.

slides.title: The phone's clock said the OTP had expired
slides.tldr: If expiry is decided by the client's clock, a fast clock cancels a valid code and a slow clock lets an expired one through. The server decides.

slides.title: Deadline vs duration: what to store, what to count
slides.tldr: Store expiry as a fixed moment (a deadline, expires_at). To count down or measure a wait, use a duration and a monotonic timer.

slides.title: The server is the judge, with a small grace
slides.tldr: Compare expires_at with the current time from the server's Clock. Allow a small grace for network delay and slight clock differences between issue and verification.

slides.title: Timeout budget: spending the whole request's time in portions
slides.tldr: Instead of a separate timeout on every call, set one total deadline for the whole request. Count it with hrtime and give each step only what remains.

slides.title: Three timeout traps: bigger inside, retries multiply, unbounded
slides.tldr: If an inner timeout is bigger than the outer one, work carries on after the outer caller has given up. Retries multiply the timeout. Without a timeout, one hung call blocks everything.

topics.title: Payments
topics.summary: Never charge twice, never lose a payment. Idempotency, webhooks and the dreaded "did it go through?"

slides.title: One tap, charged twice
slides.tldr: If a reply is lost on the way back, the client sends again; and if the server can't tell the two requests apart, the same payment happens twice.

slides.title: The check number: one check can't be cashed twice
slides.tldr: The client sends a unique key with each job; the server records the key, and when the same key comes back it returns the earlier reply.

slides.title: Building the register: key, fingerprint and stored reply
