slides.tldr: Keep one table with (scope, key) unique, and store the request's fingerprint and the response; the controller takes the key from the header and hands it to a guard.

slides.title: Claim, work, store the reply: in one transaction
slides.tldr: Insert the key row, do the real work and store the reply in one transaction; if the INSERT affects 0 rows, replay the stored reply without doing the work.

slides.title: A new key on every try: the classic mistake
slides.tldr: A key belongs to the user's intention, not to an attempt: the same key on a retry, a new key when the form changes.

slides.title: Every write: what if it arrives twice?
slides.tldr: Not every write needs a key: some are naturally idempotent, some are covered by a unique constraint, and the rest are made safe with an idempotency key.

slides.title: Who sent this "paid" message?
slides.tldr: A webhook is a POST that arrives at your URL from outside; trust it without checking the seal and anyone can fake a "paid" call and get an order for free.

slides.title: The sealed package: HMAC signatures
slides.tldr: The gateway sends a signature: an HMAC of the body and timestamp under a shared secret. The server builds the same hash itself to compare, and rejects old timestamps.

slides.title: Verify, store, then reply 200
slides.tldr: Check the seal with hash_hmac and hash_equals on the raw body, store the event and hand it to Messenger, and return 200 fast.

slides.title: It will arrive twice, and out of order
slides.tldr: Webhooks are delivered at least once and in no guaranteed order; the handler must block duplicates by event id, and a state machine must stop old news from moving a payment backwards.

slides.title: An early event must not be thrown away
slides.tldr: If the payment is not ready for an event yet, rejecting it and marking it processed loses it for good. Roll back and retry; drop only events the payment has already moved past.

slides.title: A status that anyone can write anything into
slides.tldr: If a payment's status is a plain string that any code can set, a failed payment gets refunded and a successful one slips back to pending.

slides.title: The ticket's life: states, transitions and terminals
slides.tldr: Draw the payment's legal states and the legal transitions between them up front; nothing leaves failed or refunded.

slides.title: Putting the diagram into code with Symfony Workflow
slides.tldr: Describe places and transitions under framework.workflows with type: state_machine; then calling can() and apply() rejects an illegal change on the spot.

slides.title: Two workers at once: can() is not enough
slides.tldr: can() and apply() work in memory; if two workers read the same pending payment together, both think they are legal. Use a database lock or a conditional UPDATE to make the change atomic.

slides.title: A timeout, and nobody knows whether the money moved
slides.tldr: When a gateway call times out, it may have succeeded, failed or be unknown; treat a timeout as failure and retry, and the customer is charged twice.

slides.title: No confirmation, but the balance went down
slides.tldr: Give the unknown state its own place (pending), then take your time asking the gateway for the truth or wait for its webhook; never guess.

slides.title: Stay pending, and retry with the same key
slides.tldr: Commit the payment as pending before calling the gateway; on a transport error or 5xx, don't fail it but verify later; and on a retry, send the same idempotency key.

slides.title: Ask for the truth: status queries and the sweeper
slides.tldr: A CheckPaymentStatus handler asks the gateway by reference and settles the payment; a periodic sweeper picks up old pending ones and sends them back for checking.

topics.title: Authentication & Security
topics.summary: Who you are and what you may do, plus the non-negotiable rules for input, secrets and stored data.

slides.title: Change one number in the URL, read someone else's invoice
slides.tldr: Checking that the user is logged in is not enough: before returning anything, check that it belongs to this user. Otherwise you have an IDOR.

slides.title: Two different questions: who are you, and is this yours?
slides.tldr: Authentication (AuthN) checks who you are; authorization (AuthZ) decides whether you may do this action on this thing.

slides.title: Where everything lives in Symfony Security
slides.tldr: The firewall's authenticator does AuthN. access_control, #[IsGranted] and voters do AuthZ, from coarse to fine in three layers.

slides.title: Checking ownership on every object: the voter
slides.tldr: Write the ownership rule in one voter and call it with #[IsGranted] on each action. For lists, filter by owner in the query itself.

slides.title: Four familiar gaps where other people's data leaks
slides.tldr: Taking userId from the request, hiding buttons in the UI, treating a UUID as a lock, and checking only GET: all four are broken authorization.

slides.title: The read is guarded, the delete is not
slides.tldr: Guard every method of an endpoint, not just GET. A hidden button only hides the way in; the DELETE route is still open to anyone with curl.

slides.title: Fired, but the token still works
slides.tldr: Once a self-contained JWT is issued, the server can't take it back before it expires. That is the revocation problem.

slides.title: A name on a guest list, or a printed ticket?
slides.tldr: A session keeps state on the server (easy to revoke). A JWT carries state in the token (stateless, but hard to revoke).

slides.title: Short-lived access tokens and refresh tokens
slides.tldr: The access token is a signed JWT that lasts 15 minutes. The refresh token lasts long, is single-use and stored hashed in the database, so a theft does limited damage.

slides.title: What a ban costs: up to 15 minutes
slides.tldr: With short tokens a ban bites within 15 minutes, not 29 days. If that is too slow, you pay with a lookup on every request.

slides.title: Where to keep the token: not localStorage
slides.tldr: Any XSS can read a token in localStorage. An HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie is out of JavaScript's reach.

slides.title: A new app asks for your Gmail password
slides.tldr: Handing your password to another app hands over all your power. OAuth2 gives limited, expiring, revocable permission instead.

slides.title: Who is involved, and what OAuth2, OIDC and SAML are each for
slides.tldr: OAuth2 grants permission (authorization). OIDC adds "who is this" on top. SAML does the same job in an older XML style, for corporate SSO.

slides.title: Authorization code + PKCE, step by step
slides.tldr: Only a single-use code travels through the browser. The server swaps it for tokens, and PKCE's code_verifier proves that the same party started the flow.

slides.title: The user is back: trust nothing you haven't verified
slides.tldr: In the callback, check state, exchange the code, then check the id_token's iss, aud, exp and nonce. For API access tokens, use Symfony's oidc handler.

slides.title: Familiar mistakes in OAuth
slides.tldr: Skipping state, wildcards in redirect_uri, the implicit flow, treating an access token as login, and a client secret in an SPA: all five break OAuth.

slides.title: From ROLE_MANAGER to 40 roles
slides.tldr: Starting with roles alone is easy. But once conditions like "own department, expenses under $500" arrive, the number of roles explodes.

slides.title: Titles, conditions and relationships: three kinds of rules
slides.tldr: RBAC looks at titles, ABAC at facts about the user, the thing and the environment, ReBAC at the relationship to the thing. When rules get complex, use a policy engine.

slides.title: Role + conditions: writing an ABAC voter
slides.tldr: A role hierarchy gives the coarse permission, a voter checks facts about the thing (department, amount, owner) for the fine rules, and #[IsGranted] guards the action.

slides.title: Permission by relationship: from folder to file
slides.tldr: In ReBAC the voter climbs up from the thing (file → folder → project) looking for any grant to the user. The relation it finds is the permission.

slides.title: Four slippery spots in authorization
slides.tldr: Scattered ifs, defaulting to "yes", stale roles frozen into a token, and guarding only some actions: each one breaks the rules in a different way.

slides.title: Deny by default, guard every action
slides.tldr: A voter that ends in "return true" lets every new action through. End it in false, and put a guard on every route, export and delete included.

slides.title: One forgotten WHERE, and every company's data in one place
slides.tldr: When many customers (tenants) share one database, every query must filter by tenant. Forget it in one query and one customer sees another's data.

slides.title: A bunk in a shared room, an apartment, or a separate house
slides.tldr: Three levels of tenant separation: a tenant_id in shared tables (row), a separate schema, a separate database. The more separate, the safer and the pricier.

slides.title: A Doctrine filter: scoping every query by tenant automatically
slides.tldr: An SQLFilter adds `tenant_id = ?` to every Doctrine query for you. Enable it at the start of the request with the logged-in user's tenant.

slides.title: Registering the filter and stamping new rows
slides.tldr: Register the filter in doctrine.yaml, and stamp the tenant on every new row in a prePersist listener. The filter guards reads; this guards writes.

slides.title: Keeping one tenant from using up everyone's water
slides.tldr: A per-tenant rate limit, separate queues or worker shares, and limits on heavy jobs stop one customer's load from slowing the rest.

slides.title: Four ways data seeps through even with a filter
slides.tldr: Raw SQL, background workers, cache keys and unique indexes: the Doctrine filter doesn't reach these four places, so tenant must be handled separately there.

slides.title: Account takeover through a guessable reset link
slides.tldr: Forgot-password is a back door weaker than the front door. If the reset token is guessable, an attacker can open any account.

slides.title: A good reset token: random, hashed, expiring, single-use
slides.tldr: A reset token is random from a CSPRNG, stored only as a hash, short-lived and single-use. Without all four properties the back door is open.

slides.title: Sending the reset link: always the same answer
slides.tldr: The forgot endpoint gives the same answer whether or not the email exists (blocking user enumeration), rate-limits, and creates the token and sends the mail in an async handler.

slides.title: Completing the reset: verify, change, and close every door
slides.tldr: Match the token hash and check expiry and use, change the password, mark the token used, revoke old sessions and API tokens, and notify the user.

slides.title: More back doors in recovery, and resetting MFA
slides.tldr: Resetting by skipping MFA, security questions, passwords sent in plain email and unlimited attempts all make even strong login worthless.

slides.title: The safe's key is hanging on the wall
slides.tldr: Once a secret reaches git, it is leaked for good, even if the repository is private and you delete the file later.

slides.title: Symfony secrets vault: the locked notebook
slides.tldr: You can keep encrypted secrets in git. The key that opens them (the private key) lives only on the production server, never with the code.

slides.title: Using secrets: read them from env, not from code
slides.tldr: Store with secrets:set, inject with #[Autowire(env: ...)], use .env.local for development, and only ever use test keys there.

slides.title: When a secret leaks: replace it, don't just delete it
slides.tldr: After a leak, bring the new secret online first, then revoke the old one. And give every key only as much power as it needs.

slides.title: The feature shipped, and nobody asked "what if someone does the opposite?"
slides.tldr: Most security holes come not from coding slips but from never asking "what could an attacker do?" at design time. Threat modeling makes you ask it early.

slides.title: Trust boundary: where the level of trust changes
slides.tldr: A trust boundary is the line where data passes between zones of different trustworthiness. Almost every attack happens around those lines.

slides.title: STRIDE: a checklist of six questions
slides.tldr: STRIDE names six kinds of threat: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. Ask all six at every arrow.

slides.title: A feature's threat model in 30 minutes
slides.tldr: Four steps: draw what you are building, look for what can go wrong with STRIDE, decide what to do, and verify it was done.

slides.title: Check at the door: everything coming in is a stranger
slides.tldr: Browser checks are only a convenience for the user. The real guard is on the server, using an allowlist, and in Symfony DTOs and constraints make that easy.

slides.title: SQL injection: when input becomes a command
slides.tldr: Gluing input into a SQL string turns data into instructions. With a parameterized query the value travels on a separate path, so it can never become an instruction.

slides.title: XSS: someone else's code on the notice board
slides.tldr: If you put user-written HTML on a page as it is, it runs as JavaScript in other people's browsers. The remedy is to escape it or sanitize it.

slides.title: SSRF: making the server open an inner door
slides.tldr: If the server fetches any URL a user gives it, it can also fetch the internal network or cloud metadata. A host allowlist and blocking private IPs are the way out.

slides.title: unserialize(): the toy that starts when the box opens
slides.tldr: Running unserialize() on untrusted data lets an attacker build objects of any class, and those run code as they open. JSON and DTOs are the safe path.

slides.title: File uploads: look inside the parcel, not at the label
slides.tldr: In an upload, the file name, extension and client-supplied type can't be trusted. Check the size and real type, assign a new name, and store it outside the web root.

slides.title: The database dump was stolen. What was inside?
slides.tldr: A database leaves the building sooner or later (backups, bugs, theft). So store the data in a way that a thief who gets it still can't read it.

slides.title: Passwords: fry them, don't store them
slides.tldr: Hash passwords, don't encrypt them: use a slow, salted algorithm (argon2id/bcrypt) from which the original password can't be recovered.

slides.title: Encryption: in transit, on disk, and per field
slides.tldr: TLS for the journey, disk/DB encryption for storage, and app-level sodium encryption for the most sensitive fields. Each of the three stops a different danger.

slides.title: Envelope encryption: the key to the keys
slides.tldr: Each piece of data gets its own data key, and those keys are locked with a master key in a KMS. The master key never leaves the KMS.

slides.title: How a password ends up in the logs
slides.tldr: One "log everything" debug line copies passwords and SSNs into files that live for months and that many people can read. Log the event, not the form.

slides.title: Personal data: keep less, show it masked, keep it out of logs
slides.tldr: Don't keep what you can do without. Mask it when showing it, tokenize cards, and make sure logs don't turn into a secret warehouse of personal data.

slides.title: Tainted flour in the sack: the libraries inside
slides.tldr: Most of your app's code, often 80 to 90 percent, was written by someone else. If any one library is poisoned, it lands in your production on its own.

slides.title: Lock files, audits and regular updates
slides.tldr: Commit composer.lock, run `install` (not `update`) in CI, run `composer audit` on every build, and update in small steps.

slides.title: The CI pipeline is a key room too
slides.tldr: CI runs code you haven't read and holds your deploy keys. Never let secrets and unreviewed code meet in the same job.

slides.title: Deploy keys that expire: OIDC and protected branches
slides.tldr: Deploy only after a merge to main, and swap the stored cloud key for OIDC: a one-hour credential, limited to one narrow role.

slides.title: SOC 2, PCI DSS, GDPR, HIPAA: not rules, but design inputs
slides.tldr: Compliance is not paperwork added at the end. Which rules apply depends on the data you touch, and those rules tell you at the start what to build.

slides.title: From rules to features: what you add to the design
slides.tldr: Almost all of the four frameworks boil down to a few common features: audit logs, access reviews, encryption, erasure and export, and a runbook for when a breach happens.

topics.title: Ledgers & Integration
topics.summary: Keeping the books so not a single cent goes missing, and talking safely to outside systems.

slides.title: Looks right, is wrong: money in a float
slides.tldr: A float cannot store most decimals exactly; tiny errors flip comparisons and lose cents until the books stop adding up. Never keep money in a float.

slides.title: Count the cents, and write the currency with it
slides.tldr: Store money as an integer in the smallest unit (the minor unit), and always keep the currency code next to the amount.

slides.title: The Money value object and Doctrine
slides.tldr: An immutable Money class holds an integer and a currency, checks the currency before adding, catches overflow, and maps to two Doctrine columns.

slides.title: Split money without losing a single cent
slides.tldr: Dividing money leaves a remainder; rounding every share the same way loses cents. Allocate instead, and put the remainder in someone's share.

slides.title: Just a balance column: "Where did my money go?"
slides.tldr: With only a balance number there is no history. When something is wrong, you can't tell who changed it, when, or why.

slides.title: Money moves from one account to another
slides.tldr: Every transaction has at least two entries: total debits always equal total credits; entries never change; the balance is computed from entries.

slides.title: Building the tables: account, transaction, entry
slides.tldr: Three tables: account, transaction, entry. CHECK, a currency foreign key and REVOKE block bad amounts, wrong-currency entries and edits; balance = SUM of entries.

slides.title: The posting service: unbalanced means not written
slides.tldr: One service writes all entries in one transaction after checking debits = credits in each currency. A mistake is never deleted; you write a reversing transaction.

slides.title: Debits equal credits in every currency
slides.tldr: Adding amounts without looking at the currency lets a 500 USD debit and a 500 GBP credit pass as balanced. Each currency must balance alone; a conversion goes through FX accounts.

slides.title: The gateway says 1000, my books say 997
slides.tldr: Your own ledger and the outside statement are two separate truths. If nobody compares them, missing or extra transactions hide for months.

slides.title: The matching key and six kinds of break
slides.tldr: Join every line in the two books with an immutable reference. Anything that doesn't join, or doesn't agree on amount, is a break.

slides.title: The daily job: fetch the statement, match, write breaks
slides.tldr: Load the statement into a table, find all six break types with one FULL OUTER JOIN, and run a console command every morning with the Symfony Scheduler.

slides.title: Don't edit your books to hide a gap
slides.tldr: Updating the ledger to close a break is wrong. Open the break, find the cause, then close it with a correcting entry.

slides.title: An outside service slowed down, and our site stopped
slides.tldr: Without a timeout, every worker gets stuck on the outside call. Once a vendor slows down, your whole site is dead within seconds.

slides.title: Symfony HttpClient: timeouts and retries done right
slides.tldr: Web requests get a short timeout and no retries; queue workers get retries with backoff. Tell transport errors apart from 4xx; retry a POST only with an idempotency key.

slides.title: Rate limits: the delivery office's busy phone line
slides.tldr: A vendor accepts a limited number of calls per second. Stop on a 429, and also pace your own calls with the Symfony RateLimiter.

slides.title: Keep the vendor behind your own interface
slides.tldr: The domain only knows its own `PaymentGateway` interface; the vendor's language lives in a single adapter, so changing vendor leaves the rest of the code alone.

slides.title: The fee rise: what the adapter buys and what it costs
slides.tldr: With an adapter, a vendor swap is one new class and one changed alias. The price is extra code and an interface limited to what every vendor offers. Use it where leaving would hurt.

slides.title: Fine in the sandbox, broken in production
slides.tldr: The sandbox is fast, always succeeds and has no crowd; production is slow, failing and limited. Code tested only in the sandbox gets a surprise in production.

slides.title: Half the file loaded, then a crash
slides.tldr: Read a file without checking it arrived whole, or stop at one bad row, and you get a half load, and a double load when you run it again.

slides.title: The packing slip: checksum and control total
slides.tldr: Four gates before you read a file: did it arrive whole, does the checksum match, does the control total match, has it come before.

slides.title: Past the gates, row by row: Symfony code
slides.tldr: Verify the hash and control total, claim the file, then load row by row. Bad rows go to quarantine; parse CSV and fixed-width into integer minor units.

slides.title: Crash at row 4000? The re-run finishes the file
slides.tldr: Give the file a status (`loading` until done) and give every row a tick written with its credit. A re-run skips loaded files, resumes half-loaded ones and skips ticked rows.

slides.title: Bad rows: not silently dropped, but set aside
slides.tldr: Catching and calling `continue` makes bad rows vanish. Keep them in a quarantine table with the reason, fix them, then re-run only those rows.

slides.title: One book in everyone's hands: the shared database
slides.tldr: When several apps write straight into the same database tables, every column becomes a secret API. One person renames a column and the others break.

slides.title: Four ways to communicate, and what they cost
slides.tldr: Four ways for apps to talk: shared DB, RPC, messaging, files. The more direct the link, the tighter the coupling.

slides.title: One job, two ways: RPC and messaging
slides.tldr: With RPC you get an answer now but the other side must be up. With Messenger you leave a message and move on, and the other service handles it in its own time.

slides.title: Making "leave it and move on" real: routing
slides.tldr: With no routing line, Messenger runs the handler on the spot, so a dead warehouse still fails the order. One line of config sends the message to a queue instead.

slides.title: Which one, when: three questions
slides.tldr: Do you need the answer now, are both sides up at once, and how big is the data? Those three questions are enough to choose a style.

topics.title: Workflows & Distributed Consistency
topics.summary: Many steps, many services: how to keep data correct when things fail halfway through.

slides.title: Order saved, but the news got lost
slides.tldr: Writing to the database and sending a message are two separate systems, so one transaction can't cover both; a crash in between does one and not the other (a dual write).

slides.title: The "to be sent" ledger: transactional outbox
slides.tldr: Write the event to an outbox table in your own database, in the same transaction as the data; a separate relay sends it to the broker later, so the fact and the news can never drift apart.

slides.title: Writing the outbox and running the relay: Doctrine and Messenger
slides.tldr: Persist the Order and an OutboxMessage in one flush; the relay picks a batch with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, dispatches it on the Messenger bus and sets sent_at.

slides.title: The two tables: outbox and inbox
slides.tldr: The outbox needs an index on unsent rows and a cleanup job; the inbox needs a unique key on (message_id, handler) and a retention period longer than any late duplicate.

slides.title: Arrives twice, runs once: dedup with an inbox
slides.tldr: An outbox is at-least-once, so the consumer will see the same message twice; the handler inserts the message id into an inbox table in the same transaction to skip duplicates.

segments.title: Sagas: step by step, and back on failure

slides.title: Money taken, stock held, no courier
slides.tldr: Work spread over several services can't sit in one database transaction; if a middle step fails, the earlier steps stay done and the order hangs half-finished.

slides.title: Canceling the wedding bookings: compensating actions
slides.tldr: A saga is a chain of small local transactions, each with an undo action (a compensation); when one fails, the earlier steps are canceled in reverse order.

slides.title: Saga state in the database: building an orchestrator
slides.tldr: Store the saga's step in an OrderSaga entity; an orchestrator, as Messenger handlers, listens to events and either sends the next command or runs compensations on failure.

slides.title: Conductor or dance troupe: orchestration vs choreography
slides.tldr: In orchestration one conductor decides the steps; in choreography each service listens for events and triggers the next one itself. With many or complex steps, orchestration is easier.

slides.title: Stuck sagas and failing compensations
slides.tldr: A deadline lets a sweeper catch silence, but a timeout only means "no answer yet"; compensations must be idempotent and retried forever, and steps that can't be undone go last.

slides.title: A timeout is not a failure: the step may have worked
slides.tldr: A timed-out step has an unknown outcome: cancel it too, by its own key, before undoing the earlier steps, and refuse its late reply.

slides.title: I changed the number, and now the books don't add up
slides.tldr: Overwriting the original payment amount for a partial refund destroys history; at month end the gateway's books and ours disagree and nobody can say why.

slides.title: The return slip: don't tear the original, write a new one
slides.tldr: The original payment stays untouched; each refund is a new Refund record linked to it, and the remaining refundable amount is calculated.

slides.title: Creating a Refund record: limits, locks and idempotency
slides.tldr: Lock the Payment with PESSIMISTIC_WRITE, count the remaining refundable amount, persist a new Refund; if the same idempotency key arrives again, return the earlier one.

slides.title: Partial capture and partial shipments
slides.tldr: An authorization holds the money once; each shipment captures exactly its share as a separate record, and any share that will never ship is voided (a reversal).

slides.title: Don't hard-code the fee: compute it from rules
slides.tldr: A hard-coded refund fee needs a deploy for every rule change and drifts on floats; keep the rules in a table staff can edit, calculate in integers, and record the fee separately.

slides.title: Why is the balance 200? The table won't say
slides.tldr: A CRUD table holds only the current value, so "how did we get here?" has no answer; where that question is the heart of the matter, event sourcing earns its place.

slides.title: The credit ledger: appending events and replaying them
slides.tldr: The event store only ever grows and never changes; to know the state you replay all events, and when that gets slow you start from a recent running total (a snapshot).

slides.title: The event store and the aggregate in code
slides.tldr: A (aggregate_id, version) primary key on the event_store table blocks concurrent writes; the aggregate rebuilds its state with fromHistory() and keeps new events pending.

slides.title: Snapshots in code: load fast, replay little
slides.tldr: Save the state every 100 events; load() reads the latest snapshot and replays only the events after it. The price: one more table, and a snapshot must be dropped when the rules change.

slides.title: A separate table for reading: projections and lag
slides.tldr: In CQRS the write model and the read model are separate; a projector listens to events and updates the read model, so the read model lags slightly (eventual consistency) and the UI must cope.

slides.title: When it pays off, and the cost of changing old events
slides.tldr: Event sourcing gives you history and audit but costs complexity: projections, replay, snapshots, and upcasting when old events change shape; choose it only when history is the main requirement.

topics.title: Scaling Distributed Systems
topics.summary: What breaks when your users grow tenfold? Find the real bottleneck and scale the right part.

slides.title: Twice the servers, no faster
slides.tldr: Add servers without measuring where it hurts and you spend money for nothing: the slow step is probably somewhere else.

slides.title: Three numbers: load, throughput, latency
slides.tldr: Load is how many requests arrive, throughput is how many get finished, latency is how long one takes. Near capacity, latency shoots up.

slides.title: Averages lie: p50, p95, p99
slides.tldr: The average hides the slow requests. p95 and p99 show how long your worst-served users are waiting.

slides.title: Little's Law: how many are inside at once?
slides.tldr: Requests in flight = requests arriving per second × average latency. This one multiplication sizes your workers and connections.

slides.title: Find the bottleneck before you scale
slides.tldr: Measure how much time each step of a request takes. Fix the step that takes the longest or fills up first.

slides.title: The fix: an index, before and after
slides.tldr: A missing index made one query read 4 million rows. Add it and that step drops from 2,550ms to about 1ms, checkout from 3,000ms to about 450ms, and the next bottleneck shows itself.

segments.title: Everything on one server: the risks and the split

slides.title: One upload form, and the whole shop is gone
slides.tldr: When the app, the database, the photos and the backups share one server and one disk, a single hole reaches all of them, and a single runaway job fills the disk under all of them.

slides.title: Blast radius: split what must not fail together
slides.tldr: Blast radius is how much one break-in or one runaway job can reach. Split the box so each part gets its own machine, its own door and its own failure.

slides.title: Make the database listen on the private network only
slides.tldr: Bind the database to its private address and let in only the app subnet: bind-address for MySQL, listen_addresses plus one pg_hba.conf line for PostgreSQL.

slides.title: Give the app a database user that can do very little
slides.tldr: The running app needs SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on its tables, and nothing else. Give it exactly that, keep a separate user for migrations, and point DATABASE_URL at the private host.

slides.title: Uploads and backups: the cheap basics, even on one box
slides.tldr: Before you split anything: never let the web server run files from the uploads folder, validate and rename every upload, and push backups to a place the server cannot delete from.

slides.title: What the split costs, and when one box is fine
slides.tldr: The split adds a network hop to every query, more parts to run and a bigger bill. A single box is still fine for a prototype or a tiny internal tool, if the cheap basics are in place.

slides.title: One big server, or many small ones?
slides.tldr: Vertical means making one server stronger, horizontal means adding more identical servers. The first is easy but has a ceiling; the second has none, but your app must be ready for it.

slides.title: The rule for many servers: nobody remembers anything
slides.tldr: To run the app on many servers, no server may keep sessions, files or cache inside itself. That data lives in Redis, the database and object storage.

slides.title: Move sessions and files out in Symfony
slides.tldr: Switch the session handler to Redis and write uploads to object storage instead of local disk. Two small changes make the app horizontal-ready.

slides.title: Autoscaling wakes up late
slides.tldr: Autoscaling adds servers when it sees load, but measuring, deciding, starting and health checks take a few minutes. A sudden spike breaks the servers during exactly that time.

slides.title: Scale the database last
slides.tldr: App servers are easy to add, the database is not. More servers mean more database connections and load, so fix queries, add a cache and replicas first, and shard last.

slides.title: PgBouncer transaction mode: what it breaks
slides.tldr: Transaction pooling lends a connection for one transaction only. Prepared statements, SET, advisory locks and LISTEN/NOTIFY assume the same connection stays yours, and break. Fix: emulate prepares, go direct for the rest.

slides.title: When one box dies, everyone dies
slides.tldr: A single point of failure (SPOF) is any part that stops the whole system when it dies. Two app servers aren't enough: the load balancer can be a SPOF too, and a standby twin fixes it.

slides.title: A standby twin that takes over the IP
slides.tldr: Run two load balancers that share one IP. The active one holds it and sends heartbeats; if they stop, the standby claims the IP within seconds. keepalived does this with VRRP.

slides.title: Three rules for splitting the crowd
slides.tldr: Round robin takes turns, least connections picks whoever has the least work, weighted gives bigger machines more. The best choice depends on how uneven your requests are.

slides.title: nginx upstream and health checks
slides.tldr: Write the rule, weights, failure limits and a backup server in an nginx upstream. Add a cheap /healthz that an active checker (HAProxy, a cloud LB) calls; free nginx only checks passively.

slides.title: L4 vs L7: the address on the envelope, or the letter inside?
slides.tldr: An L4 load balancer looks only at IP and port and forwards TCP: fast, and works with any protocol. L7 reads HTTP, so it can decide by path, header and cookie.

slides.title: Sticky sessions: quick relief, lasting trouble
slides.tldr: Sticky sessions always send the same user to the same server. That unbalances the load and loses the session when a server dies. The real fix is to keep sessions outside the server.

slides.title: Add a node and the whole cache vanishes
slides.tldr: Split keys across nodes with `hash(key) % N` and changing N moves almost every key. Going from 4 to 5 nodes makes 80% of the cache miss at once.

slides.title: Put them on a circle: the first node clockwise
slides.tldr: Hash both nodes and keys onto a circle. A key belongs to the first node clockwise from it. Add or remove a node and only its neighbor's share moves.

slides.title: A small hash ring in PHP
slides.tldr: A ring is a sorted list of hashes plus a binary search. Give each node 150 virtual positions, then add a 5th node and measure how much moved.

slides.title: Virtual nodes: making every share equal
slides.tldr: With a single position per node, the shares come out badly uneven. Give each node many virtual positions and the shares even out, and a dead node's share spreads across everyone.

slides.title: Where you meet it in the real world
slides.tldr: Cache clusters, nginx upstreams and partitioned stores like Cassandra and the Dynamo design use consistent hashing. Redis Cluster is close but different: 16384 fixed hash slots.

slides.title: Two servers, both thinking "I'm the leader"
slides.tldr: When only one of many servers should do a job, you have to pick a leader. If the network stalls, both can believe they're the leader, and the job runs twice.

slides.title: Quorum: decisions pass by majority
slides.tldr: A quorum is a majority (N/2 + 1). That many members must agree for a decision to pass. If the network splits in two, only one side can hold a majority.

slides.title: Raft: choosing a leader and matching the log
slides.tldr: In Raft one leader takes all writes and sends them to followers, and a write is final only once a majority has it. If the leader goes quiet, a vote picks a new one.

slides.title: "Only one runs it" with Symfony Lock
slides.tldr: For ordinary cases, give a job to one runner at a time with Symfony Lock's LockFactory. Set a short TTL, call refresh() during long jobs, and release() at the end.

slides.title: When a lock expires: the fencing token
slides.tldr: If the lock holder pauses or slows down, the lock expires and someone else gets it, yet the first process wakes up and keeps writing. The fix is a fencing token: the storage itself rejects the stale token.

slides.title: I placed an order, but "no such order"
slides.tldr: A replica gets the primary's data a little late. During that gap a user can't see their own write, data can jump backwards in time, or events can show up in the wrong order.

slides.title: Show users their own writes
slides.tldr: For a few seconds after a write, serve that user's reads from the primary. Everyone else reads from a replica. Critical reads (money, stock) always go to the primary.

slides.title: Moving the warehouse while the shop stays open
slides.tldr: Big data can't be moved in one night. Build the new place, write new data to both, copy the old data, verify, then move reads over step by step.

slides.title: Backfill: small batches, slow pace, stop and resume
slides.tldr: Run a backfill in small batches by id (keyset), with idempotent INSERTs, and pause when replica lag grows. The live site stays fast, and a stopped job can be resumed.

slides.title: When dual write slips: the old one is the truth, so verify
slides.tldr: Writing to two places, one can fail. Treat the old system as the source of truth, repair failed writes to the new one later, and verify step by step with counts and checksums.

slides.title: The branch phone line is cut: pay out or not?
slides.tldr: When the link between two copies of the data is cut, a system has to choose: answer even though it may be wrong, or refuse to answer until it is sure.

slides.title: CAP: splits will happen, so pick C or A
slides.tldr: You can't avoid network partitions. So CAP really says: during a partition you stay consistent (CP) or stay available (AP). It is a choice per feature, not a label for a database.

slides.title: PACELC: even with the line fine, you pay
slides.tldr: Even with no partition (Else), writing with everyone's agreement across places costs latency. PACELC says: in a partition, A or C; otherwise, L (latency) or C.

slides.title: Choose CP or AP per feature in one app
slides.tldr: Not for the whole database but for each feature, ask: is wrong data worse, or no answer? Money and stock go CP; likes and feeds go AP.

slides.title: Choosing AP means owing a reconciliation
slides.tldr: In AP, both sides change the same data separately. "Last write wins" depends on clocks and silently drops one change. You need a merge rule built in advance.

topics.title: Resilience
topics.summary: Something will always break. Keep the damage contained and keep the system limping along.

slides.title: One slow API took the whole site down
slides.tldr: When the courier API slows down, it is not just checkout that dies. The whole site stops, because every worker is stuck waiting for its reply.

slides.title: How failure spreads, and where to build walls
slides.tldr: A cascading failure spreads through shared, limited resources. Two walls stop it: timeouts and bulkheads.

slides.title: Put a timeout on every network call
slides.tldr: Give HttpClient both timeout (idle) and max_duration (total), set statement_timeout on the database, and write down in code what happens on failure.

slides.title: Bulkheads: a separate compartment for each job
slides.tldr: Stop one dependency from taking every worker or the whole queue: cap the number of simultaneous calls, and keep separate queues and workers per job type.

slides.title: Pitfall: "there is a default timeout anyway"
slides.tldr: The defaults are either 60 seconds or unlimited. And PHP's max_execution_time doesn't count time spent waiting on the network.

slides.title: Let everyone in, and nobody gets served
slides.tldr: When more requests arrive than you can handle, an unbounded line keeps growing and replies come after the user has left. The server works hard and achieves nothing.

slides.title: Keep the line short and turn the rest away at once
slides.tldr: Load shedding means turning away requests above your limit at the door. The rest get full-speed service, and those turned away know when to come back.

slides.title: Cap the less important work first with Symfony RateLimiter
slides.tldr: A token bucket caps low-priority routes at a fixed rate and answers 503 with Retry-After when it is hit. It is a budget, not yet shedding: it ignores how busy the server is.

slides.title: Make it react: shed only while the server is struggling
slides.tldr: A fixed cap refuses people even when the server is idle. Check an overload signal first, and enforce the cap only while the server is really struggling.

slides.title: Pitfall: "just put it in the queue, it'll get done later"
slides.tldr: An unbounded queue hides a crowd, it does not solve it. The line grows for hours and workers process stale jobs. Measure queue depth and return 503 at the limit.

slides.title: When everyone retries at once, the service can't get back up
slides.tldr: In a partial failure, if everyone retries immediately, traffic grows and a recovering service falls over again. This is called a retry storm.

slides.title: Circuit breaker: protecting the house like a fuse
slides.tldr: A circuit breaker counts failed calls. At the threshold it stops calling altogether (open), later tries one test call (half-open), and on success switches back on (closed).

slides.title: How to retry properly: backoff and jitter
slides.tldr: Wait longer before each retry (exponential backoff), and add a little randomness to that wait (jitter). Symfony RetryableHttpClient does both from config.

slides.title: A small circuit breaker with Symfony Cache
slides.tldr: Keep the failure count and the "cut until" time in Symfony Cache. While cut, skip the call and go straight to the fallback; otherwise call, and on success reset the count to zero.

slides.title: Pitfall: retries at every layer, with no retry budget
slides.tldr: 3 retries at each layer means 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 calls. Keep retries in a single layer, and cap retries to a small share of total traffic (a retry budget).

slides.title: Recommendations broke, so the whole product page returned 500
slides.tldr: When a minor part fails, killing the whole page is a mistake. Keep the core working, drop the optional part, and the user will barely notice.

slides.title: The fallback ladder: if one fails, take the next
slides.tldr: Decide the ladder for each call in advance: live data, then a stale copy, then a default, and finally switch the feature off. But never invent anything to do with money.

slides.title: A stale copy and a kill switch in Symfony
slides.tldr: Keep every successful answer in the cache as the last good copy. On failure serve it, or an empty list, and flag degraded: true in the response. Keep core data and optional parts separate.

slides.title: A degraded UI in Vue: tell the user honestly
slides.tldr: Make core and optional calls separately (Promise.allSettled). If the optional one fails the page carries on, with a short honest note or an alternative link. If the core one fails, show an error with a retry button.

slides.title: Pitfall: the fallback that quietly lies
slides.tldr: In money-related calls, `catch → return 0` is the most dangerous fallback. A good one is a value approved in advance, logged, and not dependent on the very thing that failed.

slides.title: During a deploy, old code meets a new database
slides.tldr: A deploy is not instant. For a few minutes old and new code run side by side on the same database, so renaming one column can send users a 500.

slides.title: Three ways: rolling, blue/green, canary
slides.tldr: Rolling replaces servers one at a time, blue/green switches to a whole new environment, canary tests on a small slice first. In all three, two versions run together for a while.

slides.title: Expand-contract: the safe way to change a column
slides.tldr: Not in one go but across several releases: add the new column (expand), write to both, backfill old rows, move reads to the new one, and drop the old one last (contract). At every step old code survives.

slides.title: Backfill in the right order, in small batches
slides.tldr: Dual-write goes live first, the backfill runs after that rollout ends, a check proves no gaps remain, and only then do reads move. Copy in batches; the command is safe to re-run.

slides.title: Shut the old server down politely
slides.tldr: Take the old server off the load balancer, then send the stop signal that means "finish up": SIGQUIT for php-fpm, SIGTERM for a Messenger worker. php-fpm stops on the spot if it gets SIGTERM.

slides.title: Pitfall: you can roll code back, but not data
slides.tldr: If a release drops a column, rolling the code back no longer helps: the old code can't run. To keep rollback safe, release migrations and code separately, and write the plan in advance.

slides.title: The whole region is down, and the backup is in it
slides.tldr: If the app, database and backup are all in one region, a single disaster takes everything. A disaster plan means preparing a way back somewhere else in advance.

slides.title: RPO and RTO: how much we lose, how long we are down
slides.tldr: RPO is the most data (measured in time) you can afford to lose, and RTO is the longest you can afford to be down. The business sets both, and the lower you want them, the more they cost.

slides.title: Two branches: active-passive vs active-active
slides.tldr: Active-passive: the second region stands ready, and traffic moves there in a disaster. Active-active: both regions serve traffic, but reconciling data written in two places is the truly hard part. Cheaper options come next.

slides.title: The cheaper rungs: backup-and-restore and pilot light
slides.tldr: Between nothing and a standby region sit two cheaper options: backup-and-restore (copies only, rebuilt after a disaster) and pilot light (only the database kept running). Pick the cheapest rung that meets your RPO and RTO.

slides.title: Game day: break things on purpose to test
slides.tldr: A DR plan you haven't tested is only a hope. On a chosen day, run a failover on purpose, measure the real RPO and RTO, and fix whatever turns out wrong.

slides.title: Pitfall: it's on paper, but it doesn't work in real life
slides.tldr: A paper DR plan almost always fails: the backup is in the same place, the restore was never tested, the secrets aren't in the other region, the DNS TTL is huge. Catch these in advance.

topics.title: Observability
topics.summary: You can't fix what you can't see in production. Logs, metrics, traces and incidents.

segments.title: Structured logs, correlation IDs and traces

slides.title: 2 a.m., 40,000 lines, one lost order
slides.tldr: In a plain-text log you can't isolate one customer's story: every request's lines are mixed together.

slides.title: Structured logs: a form, not a letter
slides.tldr: Write each log line as JSON: a fixed message, with the changing facts (order_id, gateway) in their own fields, so you can search and count.

slides.title: Correlation ID: a tracking number for every request
slides.tldr: Give each request a number at the front door, and let a Monolog processor stamp it on every log line automatically.

slides.title: The number crosses queues and services too
slides.tldr: Send the correlation ID in the header of outgoing HTTP calls and in a stamp on queued messages, and pick it up again on the other side.

slides.title: Outgoing HTTP calls: stamp the header for free
slides.tldr: Wrap Symfony's HTTP client so every outgoing call carries X-Correlation-Id automatically, instead of trusting each developer to add the header.

slides.title: Traces and spans: where did the time go?
slides.tldr: A trace is one request's whole journey; a span is one step and how long it took, so you see where the delay is at a glance.

segments.title: Metrics, SLIs, SLOs and error budgets

slides.title: The average says fine, the customers say slow
slides.tldr: An average response time hides the few slow requests, so measure real experience with percentiles (p90, p99) and metrics collected continuously.

slides.title: Three kinds of metric: counter, gauge, histogram
slides.tldr: A counter only goes up (how many), a gauge moves up and down (how much now), a histogram drops values into buckets (how many took how long). Percentiles come from histograms.

slides.title: What to measure: RED and USE
slides.tldr: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for services, USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for machines. Measure these six and you catch most problems.

slides.title: Adding metrics to Symfony
slides.tldr: A listener bumps a counter and a histogram on every request, and a /metrics endpoint shows them to Prometheus. Label by route name, not URL.

slides.title: SLI and SLO: exactly how good is "good"?
slides.tldr: An SLI is a measured ratio (good requests / all requests); an SLO is its target (say 99.9% over 30 days). 100% is never the target.

slides.title: Error budget: how much risk can we take?
slides.tldr: The failure your SLO tolerates is your budget. While budget remains, ship features fast; when it runs low, focus on stability. Numbers decide, not arguments.

slides.title: The alarm that rings every day, and the day of the real fire
slides.tldr: When an alert fires daily and there is nothing to do, the team learns to ignore it, and one day the real alert gets buried too.

slides.title: Alive or ready: liveness and readiness
slides.tldr: Liveness asks "are you stuck, do you need a restart?", readiness asks "can you take work right now?". Never check the database in liveness.

slides.title: Two health endpoints in Symfony
slides.tldr: `/health/live` always returns 200 (it only proves the app is alive), `/health/ready` checks the essential dependencies and returns 503 on failure. Error details go to the log, not the response.

slides.title: A good alert: page on symptoms, not causes
slides.tldr: Page on signs of user harm (errors, slowness, SLO burn), not on causes (CPU, disk). Every alert must be urgent, actionable and come with a runbook.

slides.title: A bad alert, a good alert, and the runbook
slides.tldr: Cause-based alerts with no wait ruin sleep. A symptom-based rule with `for`, a severity and a runbook link is the one that works.

slides.title: 3 a.m.: everyone's hands in the same pot
slides.tldr: In an outage the biggest danger is often not the root problem but the chaos: five people change production at once and nobody knows what changed.

slides.title: Triage: measure the harm first, then decide how urgent
slides.tldr: Don't rush off on hearing about a problem. First ask who is hurt, how badly and for how long; then set a severity, which decides how many people respond and how fast.

slides.title: Stop it first, find the cause later
slides.tldr: Mitigation (rollback, feature flag off, scale, failover) stops the harm fast. Hunt for the root cause only when customers are no longer being hurt.

slides.title: When rollback isn't enough: the database moved on
slides.tldr: Rollback swaps the code, not the data. If the deploy also renamed a column, the old code breaks on the new schema, so change the schema in two safe steps.

slides.title: Roles and communication: who does what, who tells whom
slides.tldr: One Incident Commander coordinates (and doesn't touch the keyboard), one person fixes, one keeps everyone informed, and one writes the timeline.

slides.title: Learning, not blaming: the blameless postmortem
slides.tldr: Ask "who made the mistake?" and people hide mistakes. Ask "why did the system let it happen?" and mistakes get fixed. So write postmortems blameless, with an action list.

topics.title: Failure Management
topics.summary: Something went wrong. Now what? Restoring from backup, re-running safely and correcting bad data.

slides.title: There was a backup, but it wouldn't restore
slides.tldr: Believing your backup works is not the same as restoring it and seeing; a backup nobody has tested often turns out empty or corrupt on the day it is needed.

slides.title: Photocopies of the deed: the 3-2-1 rule
slides.tldr: Keep 3 copies of your data, on 2 kinds of storage, with 1 at another location. And a replica is not a backup, because a mistaken DELETE reaches it instantly too.

slides.title: Point-in-time recovery: back to one minute before the mistake
slides.tldr: A base backup plus continuously archived WAL lets you recover to any moment; the restore happens on a new server, never on top of the live DB.

slides.title: Restore drills: break it yourself and see
slides.tldr: Once a week, restore the latest backup into a scratch DB, time it and verify the data; alert immediately if it fails.

slides.title: The runbook: the page you read when you're scared
slides.tldr: A runbook is step-by-step instructions you can follow half asleep: who does what, which commands, how to verify, and it is updated after every drill.

slides.title: Fixed it, so replay everything: and the second disaster
slides.tldr: Replaying 4000 failed events in one go causes double processing and overloads your own systems; the recovery itself becomes a second incident.

slides.title: The backlog of letters: four safeguards
slides.tldr: Four safeguards for a safe replay: an idempotent handler, a throttle, a dry run and a checkpoint. All four, together.

slides.title: A Symfony console command: slowly, with a bookmark
slides.tldr: A console command with `--dry-run`, `--rate` and a checkpoint: it takes events in batches, dispatches slowly and saves the last id after each batch.

slides.title: Run twice, nothing doubles: and no receipt goes missing
slides.tldr: Make the replay handler idempotent, and queue each outside side effect once in a table, so a replay neither doubles it nor skips one the first attempt missed.

slides.title: Sending each receipt once, missed ones included
slides.tldr: A separate sender emails the unsent receipt rows in small batches and marks each one sent, so every event ends with exactly one receipt.

slides.title: A silent UPDATE in production: a fix that makes things worse
slides.tldr: Seeing bad data and hurriedly running an UPDATE in the console leaves no evidence, can change the wrong rows, and later nobody can tell what happened.

slides.title: Corrections in red ink: four ways to fix data
slides.tldr: Fix by writing, not erasing: a reversing and a new entry in the ledger, a rule-following transition for state, a recompute for derived data, and an audited script for the rest.

slides.title: An audited data-fix script: count, record, then change
slides.tldr: A narrow condition, a check against the expected count, one transaction, each row's before and after in data_fix_log, and nothing changing if you run it again.

slides.title: Code rolls back, data doesn't: roll back or roll forward
slides.tldr: Rolling back restores code quickly but not the data the bad code wrote; when the schema or data has changed, roll forward plus a data fix is the way.

topics.title: Interaction Patterns
topics.summary: Offline work, live updates and feeds: the three hard ways a system talks to its users.

slides.title: An offline edit vanished without a trace
slides.tldr: When two users edit the same thing offline, whoever syncs last wins and the other's work is lost without anyone being told.

slides.title: Catch the conflict: which version did you write against?
slides.tldr: Send a base version with every change. If the server's version differs, don't write silently: return a 409 conflict and show both copies.

slides.title: Five ways to settle a conflict
slides.tldr: LWW is simple but loses data. Field-level merge, asking the user and CRDTs are progressively safer. Choose by the kind of data.

slides.title: Local-first in Vue: write to the phone first, send later
slides.tldr: Save every change to an IndexedDB outbox first, send in order once the network is back, and give each change an id so sending it twice does no harm.

slides.title: Your own second edit can conflict with your first
slides.tldr: Two offline edits of one note both say "written against v5". After the first is accepted the second looks stale, so rebase it onto the new version.

slides.title: The Symfony server: match the version, send changes back
slides.tldr: The server spots duplicates by mutation id, matches the base version with a Doctrine optimistic lock, and on a mismatch answers 409 with its own copy.

slides.title: "Is it ready?" "Not yet." Every two seconds
slides.tldr: If every client asks the server about an order's status every 2 seconds, almost every request comes back empty, yet each one costs the server full price.

slides.title: Polling, long-polling, SSE, WebSocket
slides.tldr: For one-way news from server to browser, SSE is simple and enough. Reach for WebSocket only when both sides talk a lot.

slides.title: Symfony Mercure: publishing from the server
slides.tldr: A Mercure hub holds the SSE connections. Symfony just publishes an Update through HubInterface, and a cookie grants access to private topics.

slides.title: EventSource in Vue: listen, and don't forget to close
slides.tldr: First fetch the current state with a plain GET, then listen to live changes with EventSource. Call close() on unmount so connections don't pile up.

slides.title: The price of connections: scaling, presence and push
slides.tldr: Every open connection costs server resources. The hub receives once and sends to many. Presence is a heartbeat plus a TTL, and push notifications cover users outside the app.

slides.title: Opening the feed stitches together 1,000 people's posts
slides.tldr: If every feed view searches for "all posts from the people I follow", that one query is what chokes the site as users grow.

slides.title: Write-time vs read-time fan-out
slides.tldr: Write-time puts a post into every follower's feed as it is written, so reads are cheap. Read-time stitches the feed together on read, so writes are cheap.

slides.title: The celebrity problem: one post, 5 million writes
slides.tldr: With write-time fan-out, one post from a celebrity with 5 million followers makes 5 million writes. The fix is hybrid: push posts from ordinary users, pull the celebrity's at feed-read time.

slides.title: Fan-out in chunks with Messenger
slides.tldr: Fan-out is huge work, so break it up: each message takes 1,000 followers, writes to Redis, then dispatches the next chunk. If a message runs twice, the feed stays correct.

slides.title: Reading the feed: merge, and keep the order stable
slides.tldr: Feed = the user's precomputed list + the new posts of the celebrities they follow, merged by (time, id). Page with a (time, id) cursor, not an offset and not time alone.

topics.title: Testing
topics.summary: You can't test everything. Test first where a failure would hurt the most.

slides.title: 95% coverage, still broken in production
slides.tldr: Coverage tells you which lines ran, not whether they are right. If most tests sit on easy code, the bugs pile up in the risky spots.

slides.title: Test by risk: the three layers of the pyramid
slides.tldr: Lots of fast unit tests, some integration tests, a few end-to-end ones. Risk decides where to add more: the bigger the damage and the likelier the break, the more tests.

slides.title: PHPUnit: unit tests and KernelTestCase
slides.tldr: For pure calculations, use a plain TestCase with a DataProvider. For database queries or wiring between services, use KernelTestCase with the real container and database.

slides.title: WebTestCase: does the HTTP path work?
slides.tldr: Use WebTestCase to send real HTTP requests into your app: routing, validation, serialization and security in one test. Keep browser E2E tests for the main journeys only.

slides.title: The trap: mock-heavy tests and coverage targets
slides.tldr: A test that only checks "was the method called" passes even with the wrong price. Verify the outcome, use fakes, and treat coverage as a signal, not a goal.

segments.title: Contract, integration, load and chaos tests

slides.title: Every unit test is green, yet the courier API broke us
slides.tldr: Each kind of test catches a different kind of bug. When the courier API renames a field, unit tests stay green because the mock still returns the old response. That is why you need five kinds.

slides.title: Contract tests: checking the deal between two sides
slides.tldr: Write down what you expect from an outside API in a schema file. Your tests build their mock from that file, and a nightly run checks the real sandbox's response against the same schema.

slides.title: The contract file, and what a rename looks like
slides.tldr: Mark the fields you read as required in the schema. When the courier renames one, the nightly run fails and names it, instead of orders shipping at 0. Cost: you hear a day late.

slides.title: Integration tests: a real database, not a mock
slides.tldr: Run PostgreSQL in tests, just like production. SQLite or a mock hides the real behavior of unique indexes, JSONB, FOR UPDATE and migrations.

slides.title: Load tests: create a crowd with k6
slides.tldr: In a k6 script, describe how the crowd ramps up and set thresholds (p95 < 500ms, failures < 1%). When a threshold is crossed the test fails by itself, so you can put it in CI.

slides.title: Chaos tests: break things on purpose to see if the fallback works
slides.tldr: A fallback or breaker that only exists on paper can't be trusted. Inject a 503 or a timeout with MockHttpClient, and create real slowness on staging with Toxiproxy.

slides.title: The bugs that never show up when a test runs alone
slides.tldr: Concurrency, idempotency and migration bugs slip past ordinary tests, because tests run one after another, alone. Yet these are exactly what breaks in production, so they need dedicated tests.

slides.title: 10 buyers at once: writing a concurrency test
slides.tldr: Launch many buyers in separate processes, start them all at the same instant, then check that stock never went negative and exactly one item sold. The next slide shows the bug it catches.

slides.title: Read first, write later oversells: one atomic UPDATE fixes it
slides.tldr: Checking stock in one statement and decrementing in another leaves a gap where other buyers slip in. One UPDATE with `stock > 0` closes it, but only for a single row; bigger rules need a lock.

slides.title: Pressing the elevator button again and again: idempotency tests
slides.tldr: Send the same Idempotency-Key twice: the response is the same and only one charge happens. Send different data with the same key and it must be rejected. That is how you test retries and double clicks.

slides.title: Migration tests: run them on real-looking data
slides.tldr: Go back to the previous version, load old-shaped data (including corner cases), run the migration, then check that the data is intact and that the old code's queries still work.

slides.title: The trap: race tests built on sleep are always green
slides.tldr: A race test that lines things up with sleep() never actually causes the race, so it is always green. Use a start barrier, run it many times rather than once, and use real PostgreSQL.

topics.title: Infrastructure, Delivery & Cost
topics.summary: Where your code runs, how it gets there, and how big the bill is at the end of the month.

segments.title: The building blocks of the cloud

slides.title: The database door open to the whole world
slides.tldr: In the cloud one click gets you a server, and one wrong line leaves your database exposed to the internet.

slides.title: VPC, subnets and security groups
slides.tldr: A VPC is your own private network. Only the front door (the load balancer) sits in the public subnet; the app and database stay in private subnets.

slides.title: IAM: who holds which key
slides.tldr: IAM decides who may do what on which resource. Give the app a role, and allow only the actions and resources it needs.

slides.title: Three kinds of compute, and managed services
slides.tldr: With VMs, containers and serverless, your responsibility shrinks step by step, and each step has a price. Managed services (RDS, S3, SQS) hand over even more work.

slides.title: What serverless costs, and a rule to choose
slides.tldr: Serverless is cheap when idle but slow on the first call, dearer under steady load and tied to one cloud. Pick by the shape of your traffic.

slides.title: Shared responsibility: whose job is it?
slides.tldr: The cloud looks after the building and the machines. Your data, access and backup settings are always yours, even on managed services.

slides.title: "But it worked on my machine!"
slides.tldr: Set up servers by hand and local and production drift apart. A container packs the code and its environment together.

slides.title: A production Dockerfile for Symfony
slides.tldr: A multi-stage build, composer --no-dev, a non-root user and a fixed tag give you a small, safe, reproducible image.

slides.title: The four core pieces of Kubernetes
slides.tldr: A Pod runs the code, a Deployment keeps the count right, a Service gives a stable address and an Ingress opens the outside door. ConfigMaps and Secrets hold config.

slides.title: The YAML for a Deployment and a Service
slides.tldr: Replicas, rolling updates, resource limits and probes: the minimum safe Deployment for a Symfony API, with its Service and Ingress.

slides.title: The trap of clicking things together in the console
slides.tldr: Infrastructure built by clicking is something nobody remembers, can't be rebuilt, and lets staging and prod drift apart.

slides.title: Terraform: turning infrastructure into code
slides.tldr: In Terraform you write the desired state, check the changes with plan, review them, then apply. Keep the state file in a remote backend.

slides.title: The Friday night hand-made deploy
slides.tldr: Deploy by hand and steps get forgotten, untested code reaches production, and a mistake leaves no way back.

slides.title: The pipeline: a factory conveyor belt
slides.tldr: Every push goes through the same stages: lint, test, build, scan, staging, then production after approval. If any stage fails, it stops there.

slides.title: CI and image build in GitHub Actions
slides.tldr: Run tests against a real MySQL service. When they pass, build the image, tag it with the git commit hash and push it to the registry.

slides.title: Build once, promote the same artifact
slides.tldr: Don't build separately for staging and production. Move one image forward and change only the config, so what you tested is what reaches production.

slides.title: Safe deploys and fast rollback
slides.tldr: Smoke tests in staging, approval for production, a check on rollout status, and an automatic return to the previous version when it fails.

slides.title: Three classic pipeline traps
slides.tldr: Rebuilding for production, keeping secrets on the server, and skipping failing tests all defeat the purpose of a pipeline.

slides.title: A $2,140 bill at month end
slides.tldr: Cloud costs pile up unseen. Unless you track them, the bill is the first thing that tells you something went wrong.

slides.title: The cost model: a wedding budget sheet
slides.tldr: Break the month's cost into components and separate fixed from variable, and you can estimate the number before the bill arrives.

slides.title: Unit economics: cost per order
slides.tldr: Look at the cost per 1,000 orders, not the total bill. It tells you whether the business is growing healthily or just growing its costs.

slides.title: Tags and budgets: whose cost, and what limit
slides.tldr: Put team, service and env tags on every resource, and set budgets and alerts in Terraform, so you know before the bill blows up.

slides.title: Cutting cost without cutting reliability
slides.tldr: Cut waste (idle resources, oversized instances, too many logs, needless NAT traffic) but not the safety net (backups, multi-AZ, monitoring).

slides.title: False savings: what you cut at your peril
slides.tldr: Deleting backups, trimming replicas or optimizing without measuring lowers the bill, but a single incident wipes out all the savings.

segments.title: Adding ML and LLMs to a system

slides.title: The chatbot that was confidently wrong
slides.tldr: An LLM states wrong things in confident prose. Hand it the real policy text and let it answer only from that, and keep customers' personal data inside.

slides.title: An LLM is really a flaky outside service
slides.tldr: An LLM call isn't an ordinary function: answers vary, it is slow and billed per token. Treat it as an unreliable outside service, with timeouts and a fallback.

slides.title: A safe LLM call in Symfony
slides.tldr: A scoped HttpClient with timeouts and retries, sensible max_tokens and temperature, PII stripped before sending, and a safe fallback for any failure.

slides.title: Validating output and stripping PII
slides.tldr: Validate the model's answer like untrusted input (enum, schema), and strip phone numbers, emails and cards before they enter a prompt.

slides.title: Evaluation: measure it, don't just feel it
slides.tldr: Measure accuracy with a hand-labeled golden set and measure again whenever the prompt or model changes. Pass on a threshold, not on exact matches.

slides.title: Prompt injection and guardrails
slides.tldr: Mix user text and instructions in one place and the user can give the model orders. Layer minimal permissions, validation and human approval.

topics.title: Hands-on Engineering
topics.summary: Architects don't just draw boxes. They write code, read code and measure it.

slides.title: But it works on my laptop!
slides.tldr: Code that worked once on your laptop and code that works a thousand times, even on a bad day in production, are two different grades of code.

slides.title: Production-ready means answering seven questions
slides.tldr: Production-ready code answers seven questions: bad input, failures, repeats, permission, visibility, a way back, and proof.

slides.title: From "works" to "ready": the same endpoint, rebuilt
slides.tldr: The same courier booking, now with validation and permission at the door, and inside it a timeout, an idempotency key and logs with context.

slides.title: Code review: what to look at, in what order
slides.tldr: A review is not about catching typos: first the purpose and design, then failure paths, security and tests, and names and style last.

slides.title: Why learn a second ecosystem
slides.tldr: Know only one language and you mistake its habits for rules. Learn a second one and you can see which ideas are universal principles and which are one framework's conventions.

slides.title: A week spent speeding up the wrong thing
slides.tldr: Optimize by guesswork and you burn time while the real slowness stays. Measure first, then change.

slides.title: Measure, pick, change one thing, measure again
slides.tldr: The optimization loop: measure a baseline, find the biggest slice, change just one thing, measure again; if it didn't help, revert.

slides.title: Symfony Profiler, Stopwatch and EXPLAIN
slides.tldr: The Profiler shows which query took how long in a request; Stopwatch times a piece of your own code; EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows how the database ran a query.

slides.title: Spike: a small experiment before a big decision
slides.tldr: A spike is time-boxed, throwaway code that answers one specific question (will this library handle 1 million rows?) with numbers.

slides.title: Six measuring mistakes
slides.tldr: Measuring on small data, looking only at averages, measuring in debug mode, not warming the cache, changing many things at once: in all of these the numbers lie.

slides.title: Facing 500 files on day one
slides.tldr: Read an unfamiliar codebase file by file and you get lost. The fast way is to pick one entry point and follow one job all the way through.

slides.title: Find the entry points, then ride one bus to the end
slides.tldr: Entry points are routes, console commands, message handlers, event listeners and the scheduler. Follow one request from an entry point to the end and the whole structure starts to make sense.

slides.title: Symfony tells you itself: the debug commands
slides.tldr: `debug:router`, `debug:container`, `debug:autowiring`, `debug:event-dispatcher`, `debug:messenger`: get a list of the app's structure without reading any code.

slides.title: Tests and git history: the code's written memory
slides.tldr: Tests tell you what the code is supposed to do; git blame and log -S tell you why it is this way and who knows it. Run it as well and you can be sure.

slides.title: Draw a one-page map
slides.tldr: Write down what you have understood: entry points, main services, where data lives, outside dependencies. Drawing your own map is what proves you understand.

topics.title: Non-technical Skills
topics.summary: The best design loses if you can't explain it. Decisions, communication and leadership.

slides.title: Three weeks of debate, zero decisions
slides.tldr: Not deciding has a price: features stall, the loudest voice wins, and the reasoning gets lost.

slides.title: All the good things never come together
slides.tldr: Every option gives you something and costs you something. The question is not "which is best?" but "which quality do we need most?"

slides.title: Decision matrix: weighing options on one page
slides.tldr: Write the criteria, give each a weight, score each option, multiply and add. Then change the weights to see whether the result holds.

slides.title: Deciding without all the facts: which way does the door swing?
slides.tldr: Make reversible decisions fast and irreversible ones slowly. Waiting for every fact means the chance is gone.

slides.title: The risk list: impact × likelihood
slides.tldr: You can't handle every risk. Score each one's likelihood and impact from 1 to 5, multiply, and tackle the biggest first.

slides.title: When you spot a mistake: the sooner you admit it, the cheaper it is
slides.tldr: Carrying on down the wrong path because you've already spent a lot is the sunk cost trap. Say it fast, reverse, and write down the lesson.

slides.title: One slide, four people, four kinds of confusion
slides.tldr: A sound design explained in the wrong language lands with no one. Each listener asks a different question, so each needs a different answer.

slides.title: Four audiences, four questions
slides.tldr: Engineers ask how. Product asks what changes for users. Finance asks what it costs. Regulators ask for proof.

slides.title: One design, four languages
slides.tldr: The design: after payment, the rest of the work goes on a queue. Four summaries, each written as an answer to that audience's question.

slides.title: Design doc / RFC: a decision on one page
slides.tldr: A good RFC holds the problem, the options, the proposal, the risks and the ask, all in one place, so people can read it and respond.

slides.title: Run a review, not a trial
slides.tldr: A review judges the design, not the person. With the right rules, authors don't hide weaknesses; they mention them up front.

slides.title: The design is right, but nobody is listening
slides.tldr: You can build influence without a title. Being right isn't enough; people listen to the person they trust.

slides.title: Influence without a title: four steps
slides.tldr: Listen first, then show evidence, run a small pilot and find an ally. Persuade with proof, not pressure.

slides.title: Mentoring: questions, not answers
slides.tldr: A good mentor doesn't pour out answers. They ask questions that teach thinking, meet regularly and share stories of their own mistakes.

slides.title: Consensus doesn't mean everyone agrees
slides.tldr: Consensus means "I may not fully agree, but I can live with this." No serious objection is enough; full agreement isn't required.

slides.title: When to stop arguing: disagree and commit
slides.tldr: Set a time limit, then one person decides and everyone moves ahead wholeheartedly. Only for decisions you can undo; never for safety, security or ethics.

segments.title: Understanding the business and the domain

slides.title: A flawless app, and Black Friday has come and gone
slides.tldr: Design without understanding the business goal solves the wrong problem, however good the code. An engineer's job is to turn goals into constraints.

slides.title: From business goals to design constraints
slides.tldr: Turn each business goal into a measurable quality attribute, and only then choose the design.

slides.title: ROI: which work comes first?
slides.tldr: Measure each project's cost and yearly gain, then see how long payback takes. Whatever earns back its cost soonest goes first.

slides.title: Fast or good: where to give, where not to
slides.tldr: Not every place needs the same quality. Cut corners where a mistake is cheap, but never on money, security or data.

slides.title: Legal rules: an input at the start of design
slides.tldr: Legal rules decide where data lives, for how long, and who may see it. Learn them at the start of design, not at the end.

slides.title: Worked example: the five questions for a small loan app
slides.tldr: Answer the five questions in writing before design. Each answer becomes something you can build or check: a region, a purge job, an access rule, an audit table.

slides.title: When the wedding arrangements fall apart
slides.tldr: Even with sound technology, a project runs late if the team, the plan, the time estimates, the vendors and the hiring aren't right.

slides.title: Four kinds of teams
slides.tldr: One clear job per team cuts overload and hand-offs. The four kinds: stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem. Under about 10 engineers, one team is enough.

slides.title: Roadmap and dependencies
slides.tldr: Write outcomes, not features, in the roadmap (Now / Next / Later). Give every dependency an owner and a date, or the delay shows up at the end.

slides.title: Estimation: a range, not a single number
slides.tldr: An estimate is a range plus its assumptions, not one number. Three points per task (best, likely, worst) give the expected time and the range.

slides.title: Vendors and contracts: what to check before signing
slides.tldr: If you don't read the contract, you may have no way out later. Check the SLA, data return, price rises, liability and exit terms first.

slides.title: Hiring: a scorecard, not a gut feeling
slides.tldr: Ask every candidate the same questions, score them on the same criteria, with evidence. Otherwise "I liked them" becomes the decision.

slides.title: Everyone's going, so should we?
slides.tldr: New technology is exciting, but shouldering a solution built for someone else's problem can freeze features for six months.

slides.title: Learn the new thing, but ask questions
slides.tldr: When you see a new technology, ask five questions: what problem, what alternatives, what cost, has anyone run it for years, and can we go back?

slides.title: The five questions, filled in for Jake
slides.tldr: Run the microservices idea through the template: with real numbers, the answer is a written "no" plus the sign that would reopen it.

slides.title: What to learn so it still pays off in 10 years
slides.tldr: Tools change every few years; fundamental ideas don't. Put most of your learning time into fundamentals and a little into tools.

slides.title: Understand the purpose before you break the rule
slides.tldr: Behind every rule there is a problem. If your project doesn't have that problem, a simpler path beats following the rule.

slides.title: Your decision is still running three years later
slides.tldr: Responsibility for a decision doesn't end when you make it. Measure the outcome, look back at a set time, and don't let debt pile up.
